section.heading: 2. Functions, Limits, and the Derivative
Introduction
section.paragraph: I n this chapter, we define a function, a special relationship between two variables. The concept of a function enables us to describe many relationships that exist in applications. We also begin the study of differential calculus. Historically, differential calculus was developed in response to the problem of finding the tangent line to an arbitrary point on a curve. But it quickly became apparent that solving this problem provided mathematicians with a method for solving many practical problems involving the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another. The basic tool used in differential calculus is the derivative of a function. The concept of the derivative is based, in turn, on a more fundamental notion—that of the limit of a function.

section.heading: 2.1. Functions and Their Graphs
Functions
section.paragraph: A manufacturer would like to know how his company’s profit is related to its production level; a biologist would like to know how the size of the population of a certain culture of bacteria will change over time; a psychologist would like to know the relationship between the learning time of an individual and the length of a vocabulary list; and a chemist would like to know how the initial speed of a chemical reaction is related to the amount of substrate used. In each instance, we are concerned with the same question: How does one quantity depend upon another? The relationship between two quantities is conveniently described in mathematics by using the concept of a function.

note.title: Function
note.heading: Function
note.paragraph: A function is a rule that assigns to each element in a set $$A$$ one and only one element in a set $$B$$ .

section.paragraph: The set $$A$$ is called the domain of the function. It is customary to denote a function by a letter of the alphabet, such as the letter $$f$$ . If $$x$$ is an element in the domain of a function $$f$$ , then the element in $$B$$ that $$f$$ associates with $$x$$ is written $$f(x)$$ (read “ $$f$$ of $$x$$ ”) and is called the value of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . The set comprising all the values assumed by $$y = f(x)$$ as $$x$$ takes on all possible values in its domain is called the range of the function $$f$$ .

We can think of a function $$f$$ as a machine. The domain is the set of inputs (raw material) for the machine, the rule describes how the input is to be processed, and the values of the function are the outputs of the machine (Figure 1).

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a rectangle labeled f with two funnels. One funnel is feeding into it at the top, with a downward arrow labeled Input x marking the entry into the rectangle. The other funnel, providing an exit, is at the bottom, with a downward arrow labeled f(x) Output marking the exit out of the rectangle.

figure.caption: A function machine

section.paragraph: We can also think of a function $$f$$ as a mapping in which an element $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ is mapped onto a unique element $$f(x)$$ in $$B$$ (Figure 2).

image.alt: Details An illustration shows two approximately oval shaped areas A and B, where A is on the left and B is on the right. Area A has a point labeled x and Area B has a point labeled f(x). A curving line runs from x to f(x).

figure.caption: The function $$f$$ viewed as a mapping

list.item: The output $$f(x)$$ associated with an input $$x$$ is unique. To appreciate the importance of this uniqueness property, consider a rule that associates with each item $$x$$ in a department store its selling price $$y$$ . Then, each $$x$$ must correspond to one and only one $$y$$ . Notice, however, that different $$x$$ ’s may be associated with the same $$y$$ . In the context of the present example, this says that different items may have the same price.
Although the sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ that appear in the definition of a function may be quite arbitrary, in this book they will denote sets of real numbers.

note.title: Applied Example 2. Profit Functions
note.heading: Applied Example 2. Profit Functions
note.paragraph: ThermoMaster manufactures an indoor–outdoor thermometer at its Mexican subsidiary. Management estimates that the profit (in dollars) realizable by ThermoMaster in the manufacture and sale of $$x$$ thermometers per week is
Find ThermoMaster’s weekly profit if its level of production is (a) $$1000$$ thermometers per week and (b) $$2000$$ thermometers per week.
note.heading: Solution

list.item: The weekly profit when the level of production is $$1000$$ units per week is found by evaluating the profit function $$P$$ at $$x = 1000$$ . Thus, $$P(1000) = - 0.001(1000)^{2} + 8(1000) - 5000 = 2000$$ or $$\$ 2000$$ .
When the level of production is $$2000$$ units per week, the weekly profit is given by $$P(2000) = - 0.001(2000)^{2} + 8(2000) - 5000 = 7000$$ or $$\$ 7000$$ .

section.heading: Determining the Domain of a Function
section.paragraph: Suppose we are given the function $$y = f(x)$$ .* Then, the variable $$x$$ is called the independent variable . The variable $$y$$ , whose value depends on $$x$$ , is called the dependent variable .
It is customary to refer to a function $$f$$ as $$f(x)$$ or by the equation $$y = f(x)$$ defining the function.

To determine the domain of a function, we need to find what restrictions, if any, are to be placed on the independent variable $$x$$ . In general, if a function is defined by a rule relating $$x$$ to $$f(x)$$ without specific mention of its domain, it is understood that the domain will consist of all values of $$x$$ for which $$f(x)$$ is a real number. In this connection, you should keep in mind that

list.item: (1) division by zero is not permitted and
(2) the even root of a negative number is not a real number.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the domain of each function.
example.heading: Solution

list.item: Since the square root of a negative number is not a real number, it is necessary that $$x - 1 \geq 0$$ . The inequality is satisfied by the set of real numbers $$x \geq 1$$ . Thus, the domain of $$f$$ is the interval $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ .

The only restriction on $$x$$ is that $$x^{2} - 4$$ be different from zero, since division by zero is not allowed. But $$(x^{2} - 4) = (x + 2)(x - 2) = 0$$ if $$x = - 2$$ or $$x = 2$$ . Thus, the domain of $$f$$ in this case consists of the intervals $$( - \infty, - 2)$$ , $$( - 2,2)$$ , and $$(2,\infty)$$ .
Here, any real number satisfies the equation, so the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers.

section.paragraph: In many practical applications, the domain of a function is dictated by the nature of the problem, as illustrated in Example 4.

note.title: Applied Example 4. Packaging
note.heading: Applied Example 4. Packaging
note.paragraph: An open box is to be made from a rectangular piece of cardboard $$16$$ inches long and $$10$$ inches wide by cutting away identical squares ( $$x$$ inches by $$x$$ inches) from each corner and folding up the resulting flaps (Figure 3). Find an expression that gives the volume $$V$$ of the box as a function of $$x$$ . What is the domain of the function?

image.alt: Details Two illustrations: Figure a shows a 16 by 10 inch rectangular cardboard. A line is drawn parallel to each of the four sides to mark a margin x inches wide all along the sides. Thus a square of side x inches appears at each corner of the rectangle. The margin lines form an inner rectangle that is 16 minus 2x inches long and 10 minus 2x inches wide. Figure b shows a cuboid that is 16 minus 2x inches long and 10 minus 2x inches wide and x inches high.

note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: The dimensions of the box are $$(10 - 2x)$$ inches by $$(16 - 2x)$$ inches by $$x$$ inches, so its volume (in cubic inches) is given by
$$\begin{array}{l} {V = f{(x) = (16 - 2x)(10 - 2x)x {{Length} \cdot {width} \cdot {height}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {(160 - 52x + 4x^{2})}x} \\ {\phantom{V}{= 4x^{3} - 52x^{2} + 160x}} \end{array}$$
Since the length of each side of the box must be greater than or equal to zero, we see that
$$16 - 2x \geq 0 10 - 2x \geq 0 x \geq 0$$
simultaneously; that is,
$$x \leq 8 x \leq 5 x \geq 0$$
All three inequalities are satisfied simultaneously provided that $$0 \leq x \leq 5$$ . Thus, the domain of the function $$f$$ is the interval $$\lbrack 0,5\rbrack$$ .

section.heading: Graphs of Functions
section.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a function with domain $$A$$ , then corresponding to each real number $$x$$ in $$A$$ , there is precisely one real number $$f(x)$$ . We can also express this fact by using ordered pairs of real numbers. Write each number $$x$$ in $$A$$ as the first member of an ordered pair and each number $$f(x)$$ corresponding to $$x$$ as the second member of the ordered pair. This gives exactly one ordered pair $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ for each $$x$$ in $$A$$ .

Observe that the condition that there be one and only one number $$f(x)$$ corresponding to each number $$x$$ in $$A$$ translates into the requirement that no two distinct ordered pairs have the same first number.
Since ordered pairs of real numbers correspond to points in the plane, we have found a way to exhibit a function graphically.

note.source_type: Graph of a Function of One Variable
note.title: Graph of a Function of One Variable
note.heading: Graph of a Function of One Variable
note.paragraph: The graph of a function $$f$$ is the set of all points $$(x,y)$$ in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane such that $$x$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ and $$y = f(x)$$ .

section.paragraph: Figure 4 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ . Observe that the $$y$$ -coordinate of the point $$(x,y)$$ on the graph of $$f$$ gives the height of that point (the distance above the $$x$$ -axis), if $$f(x)$$ is positive. If $$f(x)$$ is negative, then $$- f(x)$$ gives the depth of the point $$(x,y)$$ (the distance below the $$x$$ -axis). Also, observe that the domain of $$f$$ is a set of real numbers lying on the $$x$$ -axis, whereas the range of $$f$$ lies on the $$y$$ -axis.

The perpendicular to the horizontal axis is at point x and the perpendicular to the vertical axis is at point y. The path of the curve labeled y = f (x) is as follows: It begins in the fourth quadrant near the vertical axis, slopes downward to the right, bulges away from the x axis, reaches the low point, where it turns to extend upward, passes through the x axis, and crosses the first quadrant, goes up, bulges away from the x axis, passes through the point (x, y) and reaches an unlabeled point above to the right of (x, y).The numbers which lie on the x axis throughout the curve is domain and the numbers on the y axis throughout the curve is range.

example.heading: Solution

list.item: From the graph of $$f$$ , we see that $$y = - 2$$ when $$x = 3$$ , and we conclude that $$f(3) = - 2$$ . Similarly, we see that $$f(5) = 3$$ .

Since the point $$(3, - 2)$$ lies below the $$x$$ -axis, we see that the depth of the point $$\left( 3,f(3) \right)$$ is $$- f(3) = - ( - 2) = 2$$ units below the $$x$$ -axis. The point $$\left( 5,f(5) \right)$$ lies above the $$x$$ -axis and is located at a height of $$f(5)$$ , or $$3$$ units above the $$x$$ -axis.

Observe that $$x$$ may take on all values between $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 7$$ , inclusive, so the domain of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack - 1,7\rbrack$$ . Next, observe that as $$x$$ takes on all values in the domain of $$f$$ , $$f(x)$$ takes on all values between $$- 2$$ and $$7$$ , inclusive. (You can easily see this by running your index finger along the $$x$$ -axis from $$x = - 1$$ to $$x = 7$$ and observing the corresponding values assumed by the $$y$$ -coordinate of each point of the graph of $$f$$ .) Therefore, the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack - 2,7\rbrack$$ .

section.paragraph: We can gain much information about the graph of a function by plotting a few points on its graph. Later on, we will develop more systematic and sophisticated techniques for graphing functions.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The domain of the function is the set of all real numbers. By assigning several values to the variable $$x$$ and computing the corresponding values for $$y$$ , we obtain the following solutions to the equation $$y = x^{2} + 1$$ :

By plotting these points and then connecting them with a smooth curve, we obtain the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ , which is a parabola (Figure 6). To determine the range of $$f$$ , we observe that $$x^{2} \geq 0$$ if $$x$$ is any real number, and so $$x^{2} + 1 \geq 1$$ for all real numbers $$x$$ . We conclude that the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ . The graph of $$f$$ confirms this result visually.

section.paragraph: Sometimes a function is defined by giving different formulas for different parts of its domain. Such a function is said to be a piecewise-defined function.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The function $$f$$ is defined in a piecewise fashion on the set of all real numbers. In the subdomain $$( - \infty,0)$$ , the rule for $$f$$ is given by $$f(x) = - x$$ . The equation $$y = - x$$ is a linear equation in the slope-intercept form (with slope $$- 1$$ and intercept $$0$$ ). Therefore, the graph of $$f$$ corresponding to the subdomain $$( - \infty,0)$$ is the half-line shown in Figure 7. Next, in the subdomain $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ , the rule for $$f$$ is given by $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . section.heading: The Vertical Line Test
section.paragraph: Although it is true that every function $$f$$ of a variable $$x$$ has a graph in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, it is not true that every curve in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the graph of a function. For example, consider the curve depicted in Figure 9. This is the graph of the equation $$y^{2} = x$$ . In general, the graph of an equation is the set of all ordered pairs $$(x,y)$$ that satisfy the given equation. Observe that the points $$(9, - 3)$$ and $$(9,3)$$ both lie on the curve. This implies that the number $$x = 9$$ is associated with two numbers: $$y = - 3$$ and $$y = 3$$ . But this clearly violates the uniqueness property of a function. Thus, we conclude that the curve under consideration cannot be the graph of a function.

image.alt: Details A line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis ranges from around 0 to beyond positive 13 and the vertical axis ranges from around negative 8 to beyond positive 8. A straight line x = 9 parallel to the vertical axis passes through point (9, 3) in the first quadrant and point (9, negative 3) in the second quadrant. The curve in the first quadrant begins at the origin, goes upward to the right, bulges up, away from the x axis,, passes through (9, 3), and continues to the right. The curve in the fourth quadrant begins at the origin, goes downward to the right, bulges down, away from the x axis, passes through (9, negative 3), and continues to the right.

figure.caption: Since a vertical line passes through the curve at more than one point, we deduce that the curve is not the graph of a function.

section.paragraph: This example suggests the following Vertical Line Test for determining whether a curve is the graph of a function.

note.title: Vertical Line Test
note.heading: Vertical Line Test
note.paragraph: A curve in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the graph of a function $$y = f(x)$$ if and only if each vertical line intersects it in at most one point.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Determine which of the curves shown in Figure 10 are the graphs of functions of $$x$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The curves depicted in Figure 10a, c, and d are graphs of functions because each curve satisfies the requirement that each vertical line intersects the curve in at most one point. Note that the vertical line shown in Figure 10c does not intersect the graph because the point on the $$x$$ -axis through which this line passes does not lie in the domain of the function. The curve depicted in Figure 10b is not the graph of a function of $$x$$ because the vertical line shown there intersects the graph at three points.

In graph a, the curve enters the fourth quadrant far away from the origin crosses the negative x axis, goes upward to the right, bulging up, cuts the y axis, slopes downward to the right in the first quadrant, bulging down till it reaches the vertical line, then it goes upward the right, bulging down and extends. In graph b, the S-shaped curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. From there, the curve continues to slope linearly upward to the right, passes through the vertical line and extends further.

section.heading: Using Technology Graphing a Function
section.paragraph: Most of the graphs of functions in this book can be plotted with the help of a graphing utility. Furthermore, a graphing utility can be used to analyze the nature of a function. However, the amount and accuracy of the information obtained by using a graphing utility depend on the experience and sophistication of the user. As you progress through this book, you will see that the more knowledge of calculus you gain, the more effective the graphing utility will prove to be as a tool in problem solving.
section.heading: Finding a Suitable Viewing Window
section.paragraph: The first step in plotting the graph of a function with a graphing utility is to select a suitable viewing window. We usually do this by experimenting. For example, you might first plot the graph using the standard viewing window $$\lbrack - 10,10\rbrack$$ by $$\lbrack - 10,10\rbrack$$ . If necessary, you then might adjust the viewing window by enlarging it or reducing it to obtain a sufficiently complete view of the graph or at least the portion of the graph that is of interest.

section.heading: 2.2. The Algebra of Functions
The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions
section.paragraph: Let $$S(t)$$ and $$R(t)$$ denote the federal government’s spending and revenue, respectively, at any time $$t$$ , measured in billions of dollars. The graphs of these functions for the period between 2006 and 2012 are shown in Figure 11.

figure.caption: $$R(t) - S(t)$$ gives the federal budget deficit (surplus) at any time $$t$$ .

section.paragraph: The difference $$R(t) - S(t)$$ gives the deficit (surplus) in billions of dollars at any time $$t$$ if $$R(t) - S(t)$$ is negative (positive). This observation suggests that we can define a function $$D$$ whose value at any time $$t$$ is given by $$R(t) - S(t)$$ . The function $$D$$ , the difference of the two functions $$R$$ and $$S$$ , is written $$D = R - S$$ and may be called the “deficit (surplus) function,” since it gives the budget deficit or surplus at any time $$t$$ . It has the same domain as the functions $$S$$ and $$R$$ . The graph of the function $$D$$ is shown in Figure 12.

section.paragraph: Most functions are built up from other, generally simpler, functions. For example, we may view the function $$f(x) = 2x + 4$$ as the sum of the two functions $$g(x) = 2x$$ and $$h(x) = 4$$ . The function $$g(x) = 2x$$ may in turn be viewed as the product of the functions $$p(x) = 2$$ and $$q(x) = x$$ .
In general, given the functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ , we define the sum $$f + g$$ , the difference $$f - g$$ , the product $$\mathit{fg}$$ , and the quotient $$f \slash g$$ of $$f$$ and $$g$$ as follows.

note.source_type: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions
note.title: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions
note.heading: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions with domains $$A$$ and $$B$$ , respectively. Then the sum $$f + g$$ , difference $$f - g$$ , and product $$\mathit{fg}$$ of $$f$$ and $$g$$ are functions with domain $$A \cap B$$ * and rule given by
$$\begin{array}{rcl} {(f + g)(x)} & = & {{f(x) + g(x)} {Sum}} \\ {(f - g)(x)} & = & {{f(x) - g(x)} {Difference}} \\ {\left( \mathit{fg} \right)(x)} & = & {f(x)g(x) {Product}} \end{array}$$
$$A \cap B$$ is read “ $$A$$ intersected with $$B$$ ” and denotes the set of all points common to both $$A$$ and $$B$$ .
The quotient $$f \slash g$$ of $$f$$ and $$g$$ has domain $$A \cap B$$ excluding all numbers $$x$$ such that $$g(x) = 0$$ and rule given by
$$\left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} {Quotient}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$$ and $$g(x) = 2x + 1$$ . Find the sum $$s$$ , the difference $$d$$ , the product $$p$$ , and the quotient $$q$$ of the functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Since the domain of $$f$$ is $$A = \lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ and the domain of $$g$$ is $$B = ( - \infty,\infty)$$ , we see that the domain of $$s$$ , $$d$$ , and $$p$$ is $$A \cap B = \lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ . The rules follow.

$$\begin{array}{lll} {s(x)} & = & {(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} + 2x + 1} \\ {d(x)} & = & {(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} - (2x + 1) = \sqrt{x + 1} - 2x - 1} \\ {p(x)} & = & {\left( \mathit{fg} \right)(x) = f(x)g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)\sqrt{x + 1}} \end{array}$$
The rule for the quotient function $$q$$ is
Its domain is $$\lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ together with the restriction $$x \neq - \frac{1}{2}$$ . We denote this by $$\left\lbrack - 1, - \frac{1}{2} \right) \cup \left( - \frac{1}{2},\infty \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: The mathematical formulation of a problem arising from a practical situation often leads to an expression that involves the combination of functions. Consider, for example, the costs incurred in operating a business. Costs that remain more or less constant regardless of the firm’s level of activity are called fixed costs. Examples of fixed costs are rental fees and executive salaries. On the other hand, costs that vary with production or sales are called variable costs. Examples of variable costs are wages and costs of raw materials. The total cost of operating a business is thus given by the sum of the variable costs and the fixed costs, as illustrated in the next example.

note.title: Applied Example 2. Cost Functions
note.heading: Applied Example 2. Cost Functions
note.paragraph: Suppose Puritron, a manufacturer of water filters, has a monthly fixed cost of $$\$ 10,000$$ and a variable cost of
dollars, where $$x$$ denotes the number of filters manufactured per month. Find a function $$C$$ that gives the total monthly cost incurred by Puritron in the manufacture of $$x$$ filters.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Puritron’s monthly fixed cost is always $$\$ 10,000$$ , regardless of the level of production, and it is described by the constant function $$F(x) = 10,000$$ . Next, the variable cost is described by the function $$V(x) = - 0.0001x^{2} + 10x$$ . Since the total cost incurred by Puritron at any level of production is the sum of the variable cost and the fixed cost, we see that the required total cost function is given by
$$\begin{array}{l} {C(x) = V(x) + F(x)} \\ {\phantom{C(x)} = - 0.0001x^{2} + 10x + 10,000 (0 \leq x \leq 40,000)} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Next, the total profit realized by a firm in operating a business is the difference between the total revenue realized and the total cost incurred; that is,

note.title: Applied Example 3. Profit Functions
note.heading: Applied Example 3. Profit Functions
note.paragraph: Refer to Example 2. Suppose the total revenue in dollars realized by Puritron from the sale of $$x$$ water filters per month is given by the total revenue function

list.item: Find the total profit function—that is, the function that describes the total profit Puritron realizes in manufacturing and selling $$x$$ water filters per month.
What is the profit when the level of production is $$10,000$$ filters per month?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The total profit realized by Puritron in manufacturing and selling $$x$$ water filters per month is the difference between the total revenue realized and the total cost incurred. Thus, the required total profit function is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {P(x) = {R(x) - C(x)}} \\ {\phantom{P(x)}{= ( - 0.0005x^{2} + 20x) - ( - 0.0001x^{2} + 10x + 10,000)}} \\ {\phantom{P(x)}{= - 0.0004x^{2} + 10x - 10,000}} \end{array}$$
The profit realized by Puritron when the level of production is $$10,000$$ filters per month is $$P(10,000) = - 0,0004(10,000)^{2} + 10(10,000) - 10,000 = 50,000$$ or $$\$ 50,000$$ per month.

section.heading: Composition of Functions
section.paragraph: Another way to build up a function from other functions is through a process known as the composition of functions. Consider, for example, the function $$h$$ , whose rule is given by $$h(x) = \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}$$ . Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions defined by the rules $$f(x) = x^{2} - 1$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . Evaluating the function $$g$$ at the point $$f(x)$$ [remember that for each real number $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , $$f(x)$$ is simply a real number], we find that
which is just the rule defining the function $$h$$ !
In general, the composition of a function $$g$$ with a function $$f$$ is defined as follows.

note.title: The Composition of Two Functions
note.heading: The Composition of Two Functions
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions. Then the composition of $$g$$ and $$f$$ is the function $$g \circ f$$ defined by
$$(g \circ f)(x) = g\left( f(x) \right)$$
The domain of $$g \circ f$$ is the set of all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that $$f(x)$$ lies in the domain of $$g$$ .

section.paragraph: The function $$g \circ f$$ (read “ $$g$$ circle $$f$$ ”) is also called a composite function . The interpretation of the function $$h = g \circ f$$ as a machine is illustrated in Figure 13, and its interpretation as a mapping is shown in Figure 14.

image.alt: Details An illustration shows two rectangles labeled f and g, each with two funnels. One funnel of the rectangle f is feeding x into it at the top, with a downward arrow, marking the entry into the rectangle. The other funnel, providing an exit, is at the bottom, with a downward arrow labeled f(x), marking the exit out of the rectangle. Below the exit of the f(x), an entry of the funnel of rectangle g. The funnel is feeding f(x) into it with a downward arrow. The other funnel of g, providing an exit, is at the bottom, with a downward arrow labeled g (f(x)), marking the exit out of the rectangle.

figure.caption: The composite function $$h = g \circ f$$ viewed as a machine

image.alt: Details Three points are plotted, one across the other, extending from x to h(x), where h (x) = g (f(x)). At the center is point f(x). A curving line labeled f runs from x to f(x); and another labeled g runs from f(x) to h (x). A curve labeled h = g dot f extends from x to h (x).

figure.caption: The function $$h = g \circ f$$ viewed as a mapping

list.item: The rule for the composite function $$g \circ f$$ .
The rule for the composite function $$f \circ g$$ .
To find the rule for the composite function $$g \circ f$$ , evaluate the function $$g$$ at $$f(x)$$ . We obtain $$(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = \sqrt{f(x)} + 1 = \sqrt{x^{2} - 1} + 1$$

To find the rule for the composite function $$f \circ g$$ , evaluate the function $$f$$ at $$g(x)$$ . Thus, $$\begin{array}{l} {(f \circ g){(x) = f(g(x)) = \left( g(x) \right)^{2} - 1 = \left( \sqrt{x} + 1 \right)^{2} - 1}} \\ {\phantom{(f \circ g)(x)} = x + 2\sqrt{x} + 1 - 1 = x + 2\sqrt{x}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Example 4 shows us that in general $$g \circ f$$ is different from $$f \circ g$$ , so care must be taken in finding the rule for a composite function.

note.title: Applied Example 5. Automobile Pollution
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Automobile Pollution
note.paragraph: An environmental impact study conducted for the city of Oxnard indicates that under existing environmental protection laws, the level of carbon monoxide $$({CO})$$ present in the air due to pollution from automobile exhaust will be $$0.01x^{2 \slash 3}$$ parts per million when the number of motor vehicles is $$x$$ thousand. A separate study conducted by a state government agency estimates that $$t$$ years from now, the number of motor vehicles in Oxnard will be $$0.2t^{2} + 4t + 64$$ thousand.

list.item: Find an expression for the concentration of $$CO$$ in the air due to automobile exhaust $$t$$ years from now.
What will be the level of concentration $$5$$ years from now?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The level of $$CO$$ present in the air due to pollution from automobile exhaust is described by the function $$g(x) = 0.01x^{2 \slash 3}$$ , where $$x$$ is the number (in thousands) of motor vehicles. But the number of motor vehicles $$x$$ (in thousands) $$t$$ years from now may be estimated by the rule $$f(t) = 0.2t^{2} + 4t + 64$$ . Therefore, the concentration of $$CO$$ due to automobile exhaust $$t$$ years from now is given by $$C(t) = (g \circ f)(t) = g(f(t)) = 0.01{(0.2t^{2} + 4t + 64)}^{2 \slash 3}$$ parts per million.

The level of concentration $$5$$ years from now will be $$\begin{array}{l} {C(5) = 0.01\lbrack 0.2(5)^{2} + 4(5) + 64\rbrack^{2 \slash 3}} \\ {\phantom{C{(5)}} = (0.01)89^{2 \slash 3} \approx 0.20} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$0.20$$ parts per million.

section.heading: 2.3. Functions and Mathematical Models
Mathematical Models
section.paragraph: One of the fundamental goals in this book is to show how mathematics and, in particular, calculus can be used to solve real-world problems such as those arising from the world of business and the social, life, and physical sciences. You have already seen some of these problems earlier. Here are a few more examples of real-world phenomena that we will analyze in this and ensuing chapters.

list.item: The erosion of the middle class (Erosion of the Middle Class)
Global warming (Global Warming)
The solvency of the U.S. Social Security trust fund (Social Security Trust Fund Assets)
The growth of tablet and smartphone sales (Growth of Tablet and Smartphone Users)
The Case-Shiller Home Price Index (Case-Shiller Home Price Index)
Salaries of married women (Salaries of Married Women)
Social networks (Social Networks)

section.paragraph: Regardless of the field from which a real-world problem is drawn, the problem is analyzed by using a process called mathematical modeling. The four steps in this process are illustrated in Figure 15.

image.alt: Details Four rectangular blocks are arranged at four corners of a rectangle. The top left block is labeled Real-world problem. From this block, an arrow extends to the right reaching the next block at the top right corner. This arrow is accompanied by the text Formulate. The top right block is labeled Mathematical model. From here, an arrow extends downward to the block at the top left corner. This arrow is accompanied by the text Solve. The bottom right block is labeled Solution of mathematical model. From here, an arrow extends to the left to the block at the bottom left corner. This arrow is accompanied by the text Interpret. The bottom left block is labeled Solution of real-world problem. From here, an arrow extends upwards to the block at the top left corner. This arrow is accompanied by the text Test.

list.item: Formulate given a real-world problem, our first task is to formulate the problem, using the language of mathematics. The many techniques used in constructing mathematical models range from theoretical consideration of the problem on the one extreme to an interpretation of data associated with the problem on the other. For example, the mathematical model giving the accumulated amount at any time when a certain sum of money is deposited in the bank can be derived theoretically (see Chapter 5). On the other hand, many of the mathematical models in this book are constructed by studying the data associated with the problem (see Using Technology ). In calculus, we are primarily concerned with how one (dependent) variable depends on one or more (independent) variables. Consequently, most of our mathematical models will involve functions of one or more variables or equations defining these functions (implicitly).
Solve Once a mathematical model has been constructed, we can use the appropriate mathematical techniques, which we will develop throughout the book, to solve the problem.
Interpret Bearing in mind that the solution obtained in Step 2 is just the solution of the mathematical model, we need to interpret these results in the context of the original real-world problem.

Test Some mathematical models of real-world applications describe the situations with complete accuracy. For example, the model describing a deposit in a bank account gives the exact accumulated amount in the account at any time. But other mathematical models give, at best, an approximate description of the real-world problem. In this case, we need to test the accuracy of the model by observing how well it describes the original real-world problem and how well it predicts past and/or future behavior. If the results are unsatisfactory, then we may have to reconsider the assumptions made in the construction of the model or, in the worst case, return to Step 1.

section.paragraph: Many real-world phenomena, including those mentioned at the beginning of this section, are modeled by an appropriate function.
In what follows, we will recall some familiar functions and give examples of realworld phenomena that are modeled by using these functions.
section.heading: Polynomial Functions
section.paragraph: A polynomial function of degree $$n$$ is a function of the form
where $$n$$ is a nonnegative integer and the numbers $$a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}$$ are constants, called the coefficients of the polynomial function. For example, the functions
and
are polynomial functions of degrees $$5$$ and $$3$$ , respectively. Observe that a polynomial function is defined for every value of $$x$$ and so its domain is $$( - \infty,\infty)$$ .
A polynomial function of degree $$1(n = 1)$$ has the form
$$y = f(x) = a_{1}x + a_{0} \left( a_{1} \neq 0 \right)$$

and is an equation of a straight line in the slope-intercept form with slope $$m = a_{1}$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$b = a_{0}$$ (see Section 1.4). For this reason, a polynomial function of degree $$1$$ is called a linear function .

Linear functions are used extensively in mathematical modeling for two important reasons. First, some models are linear by nature. For example, the formula for converting temperature from Celsius $$\left( {}_{}^{} \right)$$ to Fahrenheit $$\left( {}_{}^{} \right)$$ is $$F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$$ , and $$F$$ is a linear function of $$C$$ . Second, some natural phenomena exhibit linear characteristics over a small range of values and can therefore be modeled by a linear function restricted to a small interval.

The following example uses a linear function to model the percentage of middle-income adults in the United States from 1971 through 2011. In Section 8.4, we will show how this model is constructed using the least-squares technique. In Using Technology, you will be asked to use a graphing calculator to construct other mathematical models from raw data.

section.paragraph: A polynomial function of degree $$2$$ has the form
or, more simply, $$y = \mathit{ax}^{2} + \mathit{bx} + c$$ , and is called a quadratic function . The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola (see Figure 17).

image.alt: Details Two graphs, a and b, each plot a curve on the x y coordinate plane . In graph (a), the curve enters the first quadrant near the vertical axis, slopes downward to the right, bulges down, reaches its low point and continues to slope upward to the right, still bulges down. In graph b, the curve enters the second quadrant, near the vertical axis, slopes upward to the right, bulges up, cuts the vertical axis, enters the first quadrant reaches its high point and slope downward to the right, still bulges up.

figure.caption: The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola.

section.paragraph: The parabola opens upward if $$a > 0$$ and downward if $$a < 0$$ . To see this, we rewrite the equation for $$y$$ obtaining
$$f(x) = \mathit{ax}^{2} + \mathit{bx} + c = x^{2}\left( a + \frac{b}{x} + \frac{c}{x^{2}} \right) (x \neq 0)$$

Observe that if $$x$$ is large in absolute value, then the expression inside the parentheses is close to $$a$$ , so $$f(x)$$ behaves like $$\mathit{ax}^{2}$$ for large values of $$x$$ . Thus, $$y = f(x)$$ is large and positive if $$a > 0$$ (the parabola opens upward) and is large in magnitude and negative if $$a < 0$$ (the parabola opens downward).
Quadratic functions serve as mathematical models for many phenomena, as Example 2 shows.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The assets of the Social Security trust fund in 2011 $$(t = 1)$$ were $$\begin{array}{ccl} {A(1)} & = & {0.000008140(1)^{4} - 0.00043833(1)^{3} - 0.0001305(1)^{2}} \\ & & {+ 0.02202(1) + 2.612 \approx 2.633} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$\$ 2.63$$ trillion. The assets of the trust fund in 2029 $$(t = 19)$$ will be $$\begin{array}{ccl} {A(19)} & = & {0.000008140(19)^{4} - 0.00043833(19)^{3} - 0.0001305(19)^{2}} \\ & & {+ 0.02202(19) + 2.612 \approx 1.038} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$\$ 1.04$$ trillion.

From Figure 19b, we see that the graph of $$A$$ crosses the $$t$$ -axis at approximately $$t = 23$$ . So unless the current system is changed, it is projected to go broke in 2033. (At this time, the first of the baby boomers will be $$87$$ , and the last of the baby boomers will be $$69$$ .)

section.heading: Some Economic Models
section.paragraph: In the remainder of this section, we look at some economic models.

In a free-market economy, consumer demand for a particular commodity depends on the commodity’s unit price. A demand equation expresses the relationship between the unit price and the quantity demanded. The graph of the demand equation is called a demand curve. In general, the quantity demanded of a commodity decreases as the commodity’s unit price increases, and vice versa. Accordingly, a demand function defined by $$p = f(x)$$ , where $$p$$ measures the unit price and $$x$$ measures the number of units of the commodity in question, is generally characterized as a decreasing function of $$x$$ ; that is, $$p = f(x)$$ decreases as $$x$$ increases. Since both $$x$$ and $$p$$ assume only nonnegative values, the demand curve is that part of the graph of $$f(x)$$ that lies in the first quadrant (Figure 21).

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x p coordinate plane. The curve p = f(x) starts from the vertical axis at the top, slopes downward to the right, bulging down and reaches on the far right of the horizontal axis .

figure.caption: A demand curve

section.paragraph: In a competitive market, a relationship also exists between the unit price of a commodity and the commodity’s availability in the market. In general, an increase in the commodity’s unit price induces the producer to increase the supply of the commodity. Conversely, a decrease in the unit price generally leads to a drop in the supply. The equation that expresses the relation between the unit price and the quantity supplied is called a supply equation, and its graph is called a supply curve. A supply function defined by $$p = f(x)$$ is generally characterized as an increasing function of $$x$$ ; that is, $$p = f(x)$$ increases as $$x$$ increases. Since both $$x$$ and $$p$$ assume only nonnegative values, the supply curve is that part of the graph of $$f(x)$$ that lies in the first quadrant (Figure 22).

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x p coordinate plane. The curve p = f(x) starts from the vertical axis a little above the origin, slopes upward to the right, bulging down, and extends rightward.

figure.caption: A supply curve

section.paragraph: Under pure competition, the price of a commodity will eventually settle at a level dictated by the following condition: The supply of the commodity will be equal to the demand for it. If the price is too high, the consumer will not buy; if the price is too low, the supplier will not produce. Market equilibrium prevails when the quantity produced is equal to the quantity demanded. The quantity produced at market equilibrium is called the equilibrium quantity , and the corresponding price is called the equilibrium price .

Market equilibrium corresponds to the point at which the demand curve and the supply curve intersect. In Figure 23, $$x_{0}$$ represents the equilibrium quantity, and $$p_{0}$$ represents the equilibrium price. The point $$\left( x_{0},p_{0} \right)$$ lies on the supply curve and therefore satisfies the supply equation. At the same time, it also lies on the demand curve and therefore satisfies the demand equation. Thus, to find the point $$\left( x_{0},p_{0} \right)$$ , and hence the equilibrium quantity and price, we solve the demand and supply equations simultaneously for $$x$$ and $$p$$ . For meaningful solutions, $$x$$ and $$p$$ must both be positive.

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed in the first quadrant of the x p coordinate plane. The first curve, labeled Supply curve starts from the vertical axis a little above the origin, slopes upward to the right, bulging down and extends rightward. The second curve, labeled Demand curve starts from the vertical axis at the top, slopes downward to the right, bulging down and reaches on the far right of the horizontal axis. The two curves intersect at a point (x_0, p_0), from where the perpendicular is dropped to each of the axes. The perpendiculars to the horizontal and vertical axes are at x_0 and p_0 respectively.

figure.caption: Market equilibrium corresponds to $$\left( x_{0},p_{0} \right)$$ , the point at which the supply and demand curves intersect.

note.title: Portfolio Todd Kodet
note.heading: Portfolio Todd Kodet

image.alt: A photo shows an elderly man wearing glasses with blue shirt and white flowers on it.

note.paragraph: Title Senior Vice-President of Supply
Institution Earthbound Farm

Earthbound Farm is America’s largest grower of organic produce, offering more than $$100$$ varieties of organic salads, vegetables, fruits, and herbs on $$34,000$$ crop acres. As Senior Vice-President of Supply, I am responsible for getting our products into and out of Earthbound Farm. A major part of my work is scheduling plantings for upcoming seasons, matching projected supply to projected demand for any given day and season. I use applied mathematics in every step of my planning to create models for predicting supply and demand.

After the sales department provides me with information about projected demand, I take their estimates, along with historical data for expected yields, to determine how much of each organic product we need to plant. There are several factors that I have to think about when I make these determinations. For example, I not only have to consider gross yield per acre of farmland, but also have to calculate average trimming waste per acre, to arrive at net pounds needed per customer.

Some of the other variables I consider are the amount of organic land available, the location of the farms, seasonal information (because days to maturity for each of our crops varies greatly depending on the weather), and historical information relating to weeds, pests, and diseases.

I emphasize the importance of understanding the mathematics that drives our business plans when I work with my team to analyze the reports they have generated. They need to recognize when the information they have gathered does not make sense so that they can spot errors that could skew our projections. With a sound understanding of mathematics, we are able to create more accurate predictions to help us meet our company’s goals.

note.title: Applied Example 6. Enclosing an Area
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Enclosing an Area
note.paragraph: The owner of Rancho Los Feliz has $$3000$$ yards of fencing with which to enclose a rectangular piece of grazing land along the straight portion of a river. Fencing is not required along the river. Letting $$x$$ denote the width of the rectangle, find a function $$f$$ in the variable $$x$$ giving the area of the grazing land if she uses all of the fencing (Figure 25).

image.alt: Details A diagram shows a rectangular piece of land of length y and width x, along the side of the river. Land is enclosed with fences but not along the river side.

figure.caption: The rectangular grazing land has width $$x$$ and length $$y$$ .

note.heading: Solution

list.item: This information was given.

The area of the rectangular grazing land is $$A = \mathit{xy}$$ . Next, observe that the amount of fencing is $$2x + y$$ and this must be equal to $$3000$$ , since all the fencing is used; that is, $$2x + y = 3000$$

From the equation, we see that $$y = 3000 - 2x$$ . Substituting this value of $$y$$ into the expression for $$A$$ gives $$A = \mathit{xy} = x(3000 - 2x) = 3000x - 2x^{2}$$ Finally, observe that both $$x$$ and $$y$$ must be nonnegative, since they represent the width and length of a rectangle, respectively. Thus, $$x \geq 0$$ and $$y \geq 0$$ . But the latter is equivalent to $$3000 - 2x \geq 0$$ , or $$x \leq 1500$$ . So the required function is $$f(x) = 3000x - 2x^{2}$$ with domain $$0 \leq x \leq 1500$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: Observe that if we view the function $$f(x) = 3000x - 2x^{2}$$ strictly as a mathematical entity, then its domain is the set of all real numbers. But physical considerations dictate that its domain should be restricted to the interval $$\lbrack 0,1500\rbrack$$ .

note.title: Applied Example 7. Charter-Flight Revenue
note.heading: Applied Example 7. Charter-Flight Revenue
note.paragraph: If exactly $$200$$ people sign up for a charter flight, Leisure World Travel Agency charges $$\$ 300$$ per person. However, if more than $$200$$ people sign up for the flight (assume that this is the case), then each fare is reduced by $$\$ 1$$ for each additional person. Letting $$x$$ denote the number of passengers beyond $$200$$ , find a function giving the revenue realized by the company.
note.heading: Solution

list.item: This information was given.
If there are $$x$$ passengers beyond $$200$$ , then the number of passengers signing up for the flight is $$200 + x$$ . Furthermore, the fare will be $$(300 - x)$$ dollars per passenger.

The revenue will be $$\begin{array}{l} {R = (200 + x)(300 - x)} \\ {\phantom{R} = - x^{2} + 100x + 60,000} \end{array} \begin{array}{l} { \text{Number of passengers} \times} \\ \text{the fare per passenger} \end{array}$$ Clearly, $$x$$ must be nonnegative, and $$300 - x \geq 0$$ , or $$x \leq 300$$ . So the required function is $$f(x) = - x^{2} + 100x + 60,000$$ with domain $$\lbrack 0,300\rbrack$$ .

section.heading: Constructing Mathematical Models from Raw Data
section.paragraph: A graphing utility can sometimes be used to construct mathematical models from sets of data. For example, if the points corresponding to the given data are scattered about a straight line, then use LinReg $$\left( \mathbf{ax} + \mathbf{b} \right)$$ (linear regression) from the statistical calculations menu of the graphing utility to obtain a function (model) that approximates the data at hand. If the points seem to be scattered along a parabola (the graph of a quadratic function), then use QuadReg (second-degree polynomial regression), and so on. (These are functions on the TI-83/84 calculator.)

section.heading: 2.4. Limits
Introduction to Calculus
section.paragraph: Historically, the development of calculus by Isaac Newton (1642–1727) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) resulted from the investigation of the following problems:

list.item: Finding the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve (Figure 26a)
Finding the area of a planar region bounded by an arbitrary curve (Figure 26b)

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b, plot a curve with a tangent line and a planar region on x y coordinate respectively. In graph a, the curve enter the second quadrant from the bottom left of the viewing window, slopes upward to the right, cuts the vertical axis, further arch down slightly and then plateaus at a point P. Thereafter the curve dips, slopes upward to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. A slanting tangent passes through the point P. A text below the graph reads, what is the slope of the tangent line T at point P? In graph b, a bean seed shaped planar region is plotted in the first quadrant, which is labeled R. A text below the graph reads, what is the area of the region R?

section.paragraph: The tangent-line problem might appear to be unrelated to any practical applications of mathematics, but as you will see later, the problem of finding the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another is mathematically equivalent to the geometric problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve. It is precisely the discovery of the relationship between these two problems that spurred the development of calculus in the seventeenth century and made it such an indispensable tool for solving practical problems. The following are a few examples of such problems:

list.item: Finding the velocity of an object
Finding the rate of change of a bacteria population with respect to time
Finding the rate of change of a company’s profit with respect to time
Finding the rate of change of a travel agency’s revenue with respect to the agency’s expenditure for advertising

section.paragraph: The study of the tangent-line problem led to the creation of differential calculus, which relies on the concept of the derivative of a function. The study of the area problem led to the creation of integral calculus, which relies on the concept of the antiderivative, or integral, of a function. (The derivative of a function and the integral of a function are intimately related, as you will see in Section 6.4.) Both the derivative of a function and the integral of a function are defined in terms of a more fundamental concept: the limit, our next topic.
section.heading: A Real-Life Example
section.paragraph: From data obtained in a test run conducted on a prototype of a maglev (magnetic levitation train), which moves along a straight monorail track, engineers have determined that the position of the maglev (in feet) from the origin at time $$t$$ (in seconds) is given by
where $$f$$ is called the position function of the maglev. The position of the maglev at time $$t = 0,1,2,3,\ldots,10$$ , measured from its initial position, is
feet (Figure 27).

image.alt: Details A horizontal axis labeled s (feet) is shown with 5 tick marks labeled 0, 4, 16, 36, and 400, which appear at unequal intervals as we move from left to right. There is an axis breaker between the markings for 36 and 400 feet. The time corresponding to the 5 tick marks 0, 4, 16, 36, and 400 feet are 0, 1, 2, 3, 10 seconds respectively. A decorative image of a maglev moving horizontally from left to right along an elevated track is given above the axis.

figure.caption: A maglev moving along an elevated monorail track

section.paragraph: Suppose we want to find the velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ . This is just the velocity of the maglev as shown on its speedometer at that precise instant of time. Offhand, calculating this quantity using only Equation (3) appears to be an impossible task; but consider what quantities we can compute using this relationship. Obviously, we can compute the position of the maglev at any time $$t$$ as we did earlier for some selected values of $$t$$ . Using these values, we can then compute the average velocity of the maglev over an interval of time. For example, the average velocity of the train over the time interval $$\lbrack 2,4\rbrack$$ is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} } = \frac{f(4) - f(2)}{4 - 2}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} }} = \frac{4{(4^{2})} - 4{(2^{2})}}{2}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} }} = \frac{64 - 16}{2} = 24} \end{array}$$
or $$24{feet} \slash {second}\left( {ft} \slash \sec \right)$$ .
Although this is not quite the velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ , it does provide us with an approximation of its velocity at that time.

Can we do better? Intuitively, the smaller the time interval we pick (with $$t = 2$$ as the left endpoint), the better the average velocity over that time interval will approximate the actual velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ .*
Actually, any interval containing $$t = 2$$ will do.
Now, let’s describe this process in general terms. Let $$t > 2$$ . Then, the average velocity of the maglev over the time interval $$\lbrack 2,t\rbrack$$ is given by

By choosing the values of $$t$$ closer and closer to $$2$$ , we obtain a sequence of numbers that give the average velocities of the maglev over smaller and smaller time intervals. As we observed earlier, this sequence of numbers should approach the instantaneous velocity of the train at $$t = 2$$ .
Let’s try some sample calculations. Using Equation (4) and taking the sequence $$t = 2.5,2.1,2.01,2.001$$ , and $$2.0001$$ , which approaches $$2$$ , we find:

list.item: The average velocity over $$\lbrack 2,2.5\rbrack$$ is $$\frac{4{({2.5^{2} - 4})}}{2.5 - 2} = 18$$ , or $$18{feet} \slash {second}$$ .
The average velocity over $$\lbrack 2,2.1\rbrack$$ is $$\frac{4{({2.1^{2} - 4})}}{2.1 - 2} = 16.4$$ , or $$16.4{feet} \slash {second}$$ .

section.paragraph: and so forth. These results are summarized in Table 1.

image.alt: Details Table 1 shows 2 rows and 5 columns. The row headers are t, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket. Column 1.t: 2.5, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket: 18; Column 2. t: 2.1, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket: 16.4; Column 3. t: 2.01, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket: 16.04; Column 4. t: 2.001, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket: 16.004; Column 5. t: 2.0001, average velocity over open square bracket 2, t close square bracket: 16.0004. A text above the first row reads, t approaches 2 from the right. A text below the second row reads, Average velocity approaches 16 from the right.

section.paragraph: From Table 1, we see that the average velocity of the maglev seems to approach the number $$16$$ as it is computed over smaller and smaller time intervals. These computations suggest that the instantaneous velocity of the train at $$t = 2$$ is $$16{ft} \slash \sec$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: Notice that we cannot obtain the instantaneous velocity for the maglev at $$t = 2$$ by substituting $$t = 2$$ into Equation (4) because this value of $$t$$ is not in the domain of the average velocity function.

section.heading: Intuitive Definition of a Limit
section.paragraph: Consider the function $$g$$ defined by

which gives the average velocity of the maglev [see Equation (4)]. Suppose we are required to determine the value that $$g(t)$$ approaches as $$t$$ approaches the (fixed) number $$2$$ . If we take the sequence of values of $$t$$ approaching $$2$$ from the right-hand side, as we did earlier, we see that $$g(t)$$ approaches the number $$16$$ . Similarly, if we take a sequence of values of $$t$$ approaching $$2$$ from the left, such as $$t = 1.5,1.9,1.99,1.999$$ , and $$1.9999$$ , we obtain the results shown in Table 2.

image.alt: Details Table 1 shows 2 rows and 5 columns. The row headers are t, g (t). Column 1.t: 1.5, g (t): 14; Column 2. t: 1.9.1, g (t): 15.6; Column 3. t: 1.99, g (t): 15.96; Column 4. t: 1.999, g (t): 15.996; Column 5. t: 1. 9999, g (t): 15.9996. A text above the first row reads, t approaches 2 from the left. A text below the second row reads, Average velocity approaches 16 from the left.

section.paragraph: Observe that $$g(t)$$ approaches the number $$16$$ as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ —this time from the left-hand side. In other words, as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ from either side of $$2$$ , $$g(t)$$ approaches $$16$$ . In this situation, we say that the limit of $$g(t)$$ as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ is $$16$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2}g(t) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({t^{2} - 4})}}{t - 2} = 16$$
The graph of the function $$g$$ , shown in Figure 28, confirms this observation.

image.alt: Details 6 points and a line are graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t ranges from 0 to over 3 and the vertical axis y ranges from 0 to over 20. The coordinates of five points in the first quadrant are as follows: (1, 12), (1.5, 14), approximately (1.9, 15.5), approximately (2.1, 16.5), (2.5, 18), and (3, 20). From each of these six points perpendiculars are dropped to the axes, each marks a domain. An open point is plotted at the coordinate (2, 16) and all the points fall in a straight line (diagonal).The line labeled y = g (t) = 4(t^2 minus 4)/t minus 2, enters the second quadrant from the bottom left, slopes upward slanting to the right, passes through the vertical axis at a point (0, 8) to enter the first quadrant and continues to connect all the points plotted in the first quadrant.

figure.caption: As $$t$$ approaches $$t = 2$$ from either direction, $$g(t)$$ approaches $$y = 16$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that the point $$t = 2$$ is not in the domain of the function $$g$$ [for this reason, the point $$(2,16)$$ is missing from the graph of $$g$$ ]. This, however, is inconsequential because the value, if any, of $$g(t)$$ at $$t = 2$$ plays no role in computing the limit.
This example leads to the following informal definition.

note.title: Limit of a Function
note.heading: Limit of a Function
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
if the value of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to the number $$L$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: Until now, we have relied on knowing the actual values of a function or the graph of a function near $$x = a$$ to help us evaluate the limit of the function $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ . The following properties of limits, which we list without proof, enable us to evaluate limits of functions algebraically.

note.title: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits
note.heading: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits
note.paragraph: Suppose
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = M$$
Then

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{r} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}^{r} = L^{r} {r, \text{a positive constant} }$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}cf(x) = c\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = cL {c, \text{a real number} }$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) \pm g(x)} \right\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) \pm \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = L \pm M$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)}\rbrack} = LM$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)} = \frac{L}{M} { \text{Provided that} M \neq 0}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use Theorem 1 to evaluate the following limits.

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}$$

example.heading: Solution

list.item: $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x}\rbrack}^{3} { \text{Property} 1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}} = 2^{3} = 8 {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x = 2}} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2} = 5{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}x^{3 \slash 2}}\rbrack} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}5x^{3 \slash 2}} = 5(4)^{3 \slash 2} = 40 { \text{Property} 1}} \end{array}$$

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}5x^{4} - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2 { \text{Property} 3}$$ To evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2$$ , observe that the constant function $$g(x) = 2$$ has value $$2$$ for all values of $$x$$ . Therefore, $$g(x)$$ must approach the limit $$2$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$1$$ (or any other point for that matter!). Therefore, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = 5(1)^{4} - 2 = 3$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 4}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(3)^{3}\sqrt{3^{2} + 7} {{Properties}1{and}3}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(27)\sqrt{16} = 216} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {2x^{2} + 1} \right)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {x + 1} \right)} { \text{Property} 5}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}} = \frac{2(2)^{2} + 1}{2 + 1} = \frac{9}{3} = 3} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Indeterminate Forms
section.paragraph: Let’s emphasize once again that Property $$5$$ of limits is valid only when the limit of the function that appears in the denominator is not equal to zero at the number in question.

If the numerator has a limit different from zero and the denominator has a limit equal to zero, then the limit of the quotient does not exist at the number in question. This is the case with the function $$g(x) = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ in Example 3b. Here, as $$x$$ approaches zero, the numerator approaches $$1$$ but the denominator approaches zero, so the quotient becomes arbitrarily large. Thus, as was observed earlier, the limit does not exist.
Next, consider
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2}$$

which we evaluated earlier by looking at the values of the function for $$x$$ near $$x = 2$$ . If we attempt to evaluate this expression by applying Property $$5$$ of limits, we see that both the numerator and denominator of the function

approach zero as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ ; that is, we obtain an expression of the form $$0 \slash 0$$ . In this event, we say that the limit of the quotient $$f(x) \slash g(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ has the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ .

We need to evaluate limits of this type when we discuss the derivative of a function, a fundamental concept in the study of calculus. As the name suggests, the meaningless expression $$0 \slash 0$$ does not provide us with a solution to our problem. One strategy that can be used to solve this type of problem follows.

list.item: Replace the given function with an appropriate one that takes on the same values as the original function everywhere except at $$x = a$$ .
Evaluate the limit of this function as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: Examples 5 and 6 illustrate this strategy.

example.heading: Example 5
Solution
example.paragraph: Since both the numerator and the denominator of this expression approach zero as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ , we have the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ . We rewrite
which, upon cancellation of the common factors, is equivalent to $$4(x + 2)$$ , provided that $$x \neq 2$$ . Next, we replace $$4(x^{2} - 4) \slash (x - 2)$$ with $$4(x + 2)$$ and find that

The function $$g$$ is defined for all values of $$x$$ and, in particular, its value at $$x = 2$$ is $$g(2) = 4(2 + 2) = 16$$ . Thus, the point $$(2,16)$$ is on the graph of $$g$$ . However, the function $$f$$ is not defined at $$x = 2$$ . Since $$f(x) = g(x)$$ for all values of $$x$$ except $$x = 2$$ , it follows that the graph of $$f$$ must look exactly like the graph of $$g$$ , with the exception that the point $$(2,16)$$ is missing from the graph of $$f$$ . This illustrates graphically why we can evaluate the limit of $$f$$ by evaluating the limit of the “equivalent” function $$g$$ .

example.heading: Example 6
Solution
example.paragraph: Letting $$h$$ approach zero, we obtain the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ . Next, we rationalize the numerator of the quotient by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the expression $$({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})$$ , obtaining

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} = \frac{({\sqrt{1 + h} - 1})({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}} {({\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}})({\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}}) = a - b}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1 + h - 1}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{h}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Limits at Infinity
section.paragraph: Up to now, we have studied the limit of a function as $$x$$ approaches a (finite) number $$a$$ . There are occasions, however, when we want to know whether $$f(x)$$ approaches a unique number as $$x$$ increases without bound. Consider, for example, the function $$P$$ , giving the number of fruit flies (Drosophila) in a container under controlled laboratory conditions, as a function of a time $$t$$ . The graph of $$P$$ is shown in Figure 33. You can see from the graph of $$P$$ that as $$t$$ increases without bound (gets larger and larger), $$P(t)$$ approaches the number $$400$$ . This number, called the carrying capacity of the environment, is determined by the amount of living space and food available, as well as other environmental factors.

image.alt: Details A positive s-curve and a line are graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t ranges from 0 to 60 days and the vertical axis y ranges from 0 to 400 fruit flies. The curve enters from a point little above the origin, goes up to the right, bulges away from the vertical axis at the point (10, 20) and veer toward the y axis, slopes upward to the right, bulges toward the y axis at the point (35, 350), slopes upward to the right to reach a point around (60, 400). A line labeled y equals 400 starts from (0, 400) proceeds horizontally to the right parallel to the x axis.

figure.caption: The graph of $$P(t)$$ gives the population of fruit flies in a laboratory experiment.

section.paragraph: As another example, suppose we are given the function

and we want to determine what happens to $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ gets larger and larger. Picking the sequence of numbers $$1$$ , $$2$$ , $$5$$ , $$10$$ , $$100$$ , and $$1000$$ and computing the corresponding values of $$f(x)$$ , we obtain the following table of values:

From the table, we see that as $$x$$ gets larger and larger, $$f(x)$$ gets closer and closer to $$2$$ . The graph of the function $$f$$ shown in Figure 34 confirms this observation. We call the line $$y = 2$$ a horizontal asymptote.* In this situation, we say that the limit of the function $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ increases without bound is $$2$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty} = \frac{2x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}} = 2$$
We will discuss asymptotes in greater detail in Section 4.3.

The line labeled y = 2 is graphed horizontally through the coordinates (0, 1) in the second quadrant and the first quadrant. The curve labeled y = 2 x^2/1 + x^2 below the horizontal line, enters the second quadrant around (negative 3.2, 1.8) from the top left of the viewing window, slopes downward to the right, bulges toward vertical axis decreasing to the right and reaches its lowest point at the origin, bends upward to enter the first quadrant, slopes upward to the right, bulges toward the vertical axis increasing to the right and exits the first quadrant around (3.2, 1.8) at the top right of the viewing window.

figure.caption: The graph of $$y = \frac{2x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}}$$ has a horizontal asymptote at $$y = 2$$ .

section.paragraph: In the general case, the following definition for a limit of a function at infinity is applicable.

note.source_type: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.title: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.heading: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ increases without bound (or as $$x$$ approaches infinity), written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
if $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by taking $$x$$ large enough.
Similarly, the function $$f$$ has the limit $$M$$ as $$x$$ decreases without bound (or as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity), written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = M$$
if $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$M$$ by taking $$x$$ to be negative and sufficiently large in absolute value.

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}} = 0$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}} = 0$$

section.paragraph: All the properties of limits listed in Theorem 1 are valid when $$a$$ is replaced by $$\infty$$ or $$- \infty$$ . In addition, we have the following property for the limit at infinity.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: For all $$n > 0$$ ,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}} = 0$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}} = 0$$
provided that $$\frac{1}{x^{n}}$$ is defined.

list.item: Use a graphing utility to plot the graphs of $$y_{1} = \frac{1}{x^{0.5}} y_{2} = \frac{1}{x} y_{3} = \frac{1}{x^{1.5}}$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack 0,200\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,0.5\rbrack$$ . What can you say about $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}}$$ if $$n = 0.5$$ , $$n = 1$$ , and $$n = 1.5$$ ? Are these results predicted by Theorem 2?

Use a graphing utility to plot the graphs of $$y_{1} = \frac{1}{x}$$ and $$y_{2} = \frac{1}{x^{5 \slash 3}}$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 50,0\rbrack \times \lbrack - 0.5,0\rbrack$$ . What can you say about $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}}$$ if $$n = 1$$ and $$n = \frac{5}{3}$$ ? Are these results predicted by Theorem 2? Hint: To graph $$y_{2}$$ , write it in the form $$y_{2} = 1 \slash (x\hat{}(1 \slash 3))\hat{}5$$ .

section.paragraph: We often use the following technique to evaluate the limit at infinity of a rational function: Divide the numerator and denominator of the expression by $$x^{n}$$ , where $$n$$ is the highest power present in the denominator of the expression.

example.heading: Example 8
Solution
example.paragraph: Since the limits of both the numerator and the denominator do not exist as $$x$$ approaches infinity, the property pertaining to the limit of a quotient (Property 5) is not applicable. Let’s divide the numerator and denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{3}$$ , obtaining

example.heading: Example 9
Solution
example.paragraph: Again, we see that Property 5 is not applicable. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x)$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x)$$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ Since the numerator becomes arbitrarily large, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches infinity, we see that the quotient $$f(x)$$ gets larger and larger as $$x$$ approaches infinity. In other words, the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \infty$$

Once again, dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ In this case, the numerator becomes arbitrarily large in magnitude but negative in sign, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity. Therefore, the quotient $$f(x)$$ decreases without bound, and the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = - \infty$$

section.paragraph: Example 11 gives an application of the concept of the limit of a function at infinity.

note.title: Applied Example 11. Average Cost Functions
note.heading: Applied Example 11. Average Cost Functions
note.paragraph: Custom Office makes a line of executive desks. It is estimated that the total cost of making $$x$$ Senior Executive Model desks is $$C(x) = 100x + 200,000$$ dollars per year, so the average cost of making $$x$$ desks is given by
$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{C}(x) = \frac{C(x)}{x}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{C}(x)} = \frac{100x + 200,000}{x} = 100 + \frac{200,000}{x}} \end{array}$$
dollars per desk. Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x)$$ and interpret your results.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( 100 + \frac{200,000}{x} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}100 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{200,000}{x} = 100} \end{array}$$

A sketch of the graph of the function $$\overline{C}(x)$$ appears in Figure 36. The result we obtained is fully expected if we consider its economic implications. Note that as the level of production increases, the fixed cost per desk produced, represented by the term $$(200,000 \slash x)$$ , drops steadily. The average cost should approach a constant unit cost of production— $$\$ 100$$ in this case.

problem.paragraph: Find the indicated limit if it exists.

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\frac{\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} + \sqrt{3x - 5}}{x + 2}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{2x^{2} - x - 3}$$

solution.paragraph: Letting $$x$$ approach $$- 1$$ leads to the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ . Thus, we proceed as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{2x^{2} - x - 3} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)}{\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {2x - 3} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{2x^{2} - x - 3}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x - 2}{2x - 3} { \text{Cancel the common factors} .}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{2x^{2} - x - 3}} = \frac{- 1 - 2}{2\left( {- 1} \right) - 3}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{2x^{2} - x - 3}} = \frac{3}{5}} \end{array}$$

problem.paragraph: Average Cost of Producing CDs The average cost per disc (in dollars) incurred by Herald Records in pressing $$x$$ CDs is given by the average cost function

solution.paragraph: Our computation reveals that as the production of CDs increases without bound, the average cost drops and approaches a unit cost of $$\$ 1.80 \slash {disc}$$ .

Verify your result by evaluating the limit algebraically.

The graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 2,2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ is shown in Figure T1a. Using zoom-in repeatedly, we see that the $$y$$ -value approaches $$3$$ as the $$x$$ -value approaches $$1$$ . We conclude, accordingly, that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1} = 3$$

We compute $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{({x - 1})({x^{2} + x + 1})}{x - 1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({x^{2} + x + 1})} = 3} \end{array}$$
