section.heading: 2.5. One-Sided Limits and Continuity
One-Sided Limits
section.paragraph: Consider the function $$f$$ defined by
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} {x - 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ {x + 1} & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{cases}$$

From the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 37, we see that the function $$f$$ does not have a limit as $$x$$ approaches zero because, no matter how close $$x$$ is to zero, $$f(x)$$ takes on values that are close to $$1$$ if $$x$$ is positive and values that are close to $$- 1$$ if $$x$$ is negative. Therefore, $$f(x)$$ cannot be close to a single number $$L$$ —no matter how close $$x$$ is to zero. Now, if we restrict $$x$$ to be greater than zero (to the right of zero), then we see that $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$1$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to zero. In this situation, we say that the right-hand limit of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches zero (from the right) is $$1$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x) = 1$$

image.alt: Details A closed circle and an open circle are plotted at the coordinate (0, 1) and (0, negative 1) respectively. The line labeled y = f(x), enters the third quadrant, slopes upward, slanting to the right and discontinues at the open point (0, negative 1) and continues at the point (0, 1), slopes upward, slanting to the right in the first quadrant and exits the quadrant at the bottom left of the viewing window.

figure.caption: The function $$f$$ does not have a limit as $$x$$ approaches zero.

section.paragraph: Similarly, we see that $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$- 1$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to, but to the left of, zero. In this situation, we say that the left-hand limit of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches zero (from the left) is $$- 1$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x) = - 1$$
These limits are called one-sided limits. More generally, we have the following informal definitions.

note.title: One-Sided Limits
note.heading: One-Sided Limits
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the right-hand limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the right, written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = L$$
if the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$L$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ and to the right of $$a$$ .
Similarly, the function $$f$$ has the left-hand limit $$M$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the left, written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = M$$
if the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$M$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ and to the left of $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: The connection between one-sided limits and the two-sided limit defined earlier is given by the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function that is defined for all values of $$x$$ close to $$x = a$$ with the possible exception of $$a$$ itself. Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
if and only if
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$

section.paragraph: Thus, the two-sided limit exists if and only if the one-sided limits exist and are equal.

list.item: Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)$$ exists by studying the one-sided limits of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$x = 0$$ .
Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist.

For $$x \leq 0$$ , $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}( - x) = 0$$ and for $$x > 0$$ , we find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ Thus, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = 0$$ (Figure 38a).

We have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}g(x) = - 1$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}g(x) = 1$$ and since these one-sided limits are not equal, we conclude that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist (Figure 38b). section.heading: Continuous Functions
section.paragraph: Continuous functions will play an important role throughout most of our study of calculus. Loosely speaking, a function is continuous at a point if the graph of the function at that point is devoid of holes, gaps, jumps, or breaks. Consider, for example, the graph of the function $$f$$ depicted in Figure 39.

image.alt: Details A discontinuous curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis has 4 tick marks labeled a, b, c, and d from left to right on the positive x axis with unequal interval. The curve starts in the second quadrant slopes downward to the right and reaches its low point close to the y axis, further slopes upward to the right, crosses the y axis to enter the first quadrant and connects an open point from where a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled a, the curve continues to slope upward to peak at another open point that is plotted vertically below a point, from which a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled b. Thereafter the curve slopes downward to the right to reach a point, from which a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled c. The curve continues at an open point plotted vertically above the point connecting the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled c. Further the curve slopes downward to the right and takes an upward bend to form a U shaped curve, which continues to slope close to the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled d. The curve continues on the right of the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled d, slopes upward, arching to the right and exits the viewing window.

figure.caption: The graph of this function is not continuous at $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , $$x = c$$ , and $$x = d$$ .

section.paragraph: Let’s take a closer look at the behavior of $$f$$ at or near $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , $$x = c$$ , and $$x = d$$ . First, note that $$f$$ is not defined at $$x = a$$ ; that is, $$x = a$$ is not in the domain of $$f$$ , thereby resulting in a “hole” in the graph of $$f$$ . Next, observe that the value of $$f$$ at $$b$$ , $$f(b)$$ , is not equal to the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$b$$ , resulting in a “jump” in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = b$$ . The function $$f$$ does not have a limit at $$x = c$$ since the left-hand and right-hand limits of $$f(x)$$ are not equal, also resulting in a jump in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = c$$ . Finally, the limit of $$f$$ does not exist at $$x = d$$ , resulting in a break in the graph of $$f$$ . The function $$f$$ is discontinuous at each of these numbers. It is continuous everywhere else.

note.source_type: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.title: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.heading: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is continuous at a number $$x = a$$ if the following conditions are satisfied.

list.item: $$f(a)$$ is defined.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)$$ exists.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = f(a)$$

section.paragraph: Thus, a function $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ if the limit of $$f$$ at $$x = a$$ exists and has the value $$f(a)$$ . Geometrically, $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ if the proximity of $$x$$ to $$a$$ implies the proximity of $$f(x)$$ to $$f(a)$$ .
If $$f$$ is not continuous at $$x = a$$ , then $$f$$ is said to be discontinuous at $$x = a$$ . Also, $$f$$ is continuous on an interval if $$f$$ is continuous at every number in the interval.

Figure 40 depicts the graph of a continuous function on the interval $$(a,b)$$ . Notice that the graph of the function over the stated interval can be sketched without lifting one’s pencil from the paper.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The curve labeled y = f(x), starts in the second quadrant slopes upward to the right, reaches the perpendicular raised from the x intercept a marked on the negative x axis and peaks close to the y axis. Further slopes downward to the right crosses the y axis to enter the first quadrant and to reach its lowest point, slopes upward to the right and peaks at a point higher than the peak at second quadrant. Thereafter after the curve slopes downward, bulges toward the horizontal axis, increasing to the right, reaches the perpendicular raised from tick mark labeled b plotted on the positive x axis and continues to slope upward.

figure.caption: The graph of $$f$$ is continuous on the interval $$(a,b)$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the values of $$x$$ for which each function is continuous.

$$F(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {- 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ 1 & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{aligned} \right.$$
$$G(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{x} & { {if}x > 0} \\ {- 1} & { {if}x \leq 0} \end{aligned} \right.$$

example.heading: Solution

list.item: The function $$f$$ is continuous everywhere because the three conditions for continuity are satisfied for all values of $$x$$ .
The function $$g$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because $$g$$ is not defined at that number. It is continuous everywhere else.

The function $$h$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because the third condition for continuity is violated; the limit of $$h(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ exists and has the value $$4$$ , but this limit is not equal to $$h(2) = 1$$ . It is continuous for all other values of $$x$$ .
The function $$F$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 0$$ , where the limit of $$F(x)$$ fails to exist as $$x$$ approaches zero (see Example 3a, Section 2.4).
Since the limit of $$G(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero, we conclude that $$G$$ fails to be continuous at $$x = 0$$ . The function $$G$$ is continuous everywhere else.

section.heading: Properties of Continuous Functions
section.paragraph: The following properties of continuous functions follow directly from the definition of continuity and the corresponding properties of limits. They are stated without proof.

note.title: Properties of Continuous Functions
note.heading: Properties of Continuous Functions

list.item: 1. The constant function $$f(x) = c$$ is continuous everywhere.
2. The identity function $$f(x) = x$$ is continuous everywhere.

note.paragraph: If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous at $$x = a$$ , then

list.item: 3. $$\left\lbrack f(x)\rbrack^{n} \right.$$ , where $$n$$ is a real number, is continuous at $$x = a$$ whenever it is defined at that number.
4. $$f \pm g$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ .
5. $$\mathit{fg}$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ .
6. $$f \slash g$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ provided that $$g(a) \neq 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Using these properties of continuous functions, we can prove the following results. (A proof is sketched in Exercise 101)

note.source_type: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.title: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.heading: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions

list.item: A polynomial function $$y = P(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ .
A rational function $$R(x) = p(x) \slash q(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ where $$q(x) \neq 0$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the values of $$x$$ for which each function is continuous.
example.heading: Solution

list.item: The function $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ , so $$f(x)$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .

The function $$g$$ is a rational function. Observe that the denominator of $$g$$ —namely, $$x^{2} + 1$$ —is never equal to zero. Therefore, we conclude that $$g$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .

The function $$h$$ is a rational function. In this case, however, the denominator of $$h$$ is equal to zero at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , which can be seen by factoring it. Thus, $$x^{2} - 3x + 2 = (x - 2)(x - 1)$$ We therefore conclude that $$h$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , where it is discontinuous.

section.paragraph: Up to this point, most of the applications we have discussed involved functions that are continuous everywhere. In Example 4, we consider an application from the field of educational psychology that involves a discontinuous function.

In this instance, the individual’s progress slows as we approach time $$t_{1}$$ because he fails to grasp a particularly difficult concept. All of a sudden, a breakthrough occurs at time $$t_{1}$$ , propelling his knowledge of the subject to a higher level. The curve is discontinuous at $$t_{1}$$ .

section.heading: Intermediate Value Theorem
section.paragraph: Let’s look again at our model of the motion of the maglev on a straight stretch of track. We know that the train cannot vanish at any instant of time and it cannot skip portions of the track and reappear someplace else. To put it another way, the train cannot occupy the positions $$s_{1}$$ and $$s_{2}$$ without at least, at some time, occupying an intermediate position (Figure 43).

figure.caption: The position of the maglev

Suppose the position of the maglev is $$s_{1}$$ at some time $$t_{1}$$ and its position is $$s_{2}$$ at some time $$t_{2}$$ (Figure 44). Then, if $$s_{3}$$ is any number between $$s_{1}$$ and $$s_{2}$$ giving an intermediate position of the maglev, there must be at least one $$t_{3}$$ between $$t_{1}$$ and $$t_{2}$$ giving the time at which the train is at $$s_{3}$$ —that is, $$f\left( t_{3} \right) = s_{3}$$ .

section.paragraph: This discussion carries the gist of the Intermediate Value Theorem. The proof of this theorem can be found in most advanced calculus texts.

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
The Intermediate Value Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a continuous function on a closed interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$M$$ is any number between $$f(a)$$ and $$f(b)$$ , then there is at least one number $$c$$ in $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ such that $$f(c) = M$$ (Figure 45).

Perpendiculars are dropped to the axes from the coordinates (a, f(a)), (c, M), and (b, f(b)). Perpendiculars are dropped from the coordinates (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) are represented by dashed lines. section.paragraph: To illustrate the Intermediate Value Theorem, let’s look at the example involving the motion of the maglev again (see Figure 27). Notice that the initial position of the train is $$f(0) = 0$$ and the position at the end of its test run is $$f(10) = 400$$ . Furthermore, the function $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack 0,10\rbrack$$ . So the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that if we arbitrarily pick a number between $$0$$ and $$400$$ —say, $$100$$ —giving the position of the maglev, there must be a $$\overline{t}$$ (read “ $$t$$ bar”) between $$0$$ and $$10$$ at which time the train is at the position $$s = 100$$ . To find the value of $$\overline{t}$$ , we solve the equation $$f\left( \overline{t} \right) = s$$ , or
giving $$\overline{t} = 5$$ ( $$t$$ must lie between $$0$$ and $$10$$ ).

It is important to remember when we use Theorem 4 that the function $$f$$ must be continuous. The conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem may not hold if $$f$$ is not continuous (see Exercise 102).

The next theorem is an immediate consequence of the Intermediate Value Theorem. It not only tells us when a zero of a function $$f$$ [root of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ ] exists but also provides the basis for a method of approximating it.

note.heading: Theorem 5

section.heading: 2.5. Concept Questions

list.item: 1. Explain what is meant by the statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}f(x) = 2$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}f(x) = 4$$ .

2. Suppose $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}f(x) = 3$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}f(x) = 4$$ . What can you say about $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)$$ ? Explain. What can you say about $$f(1)$$ ? Explain.
3. Explain what it means for a function $$f$$ to be continuous (a) at a number $$a$$ and (b) on an interval $$I$$ .

4. Suppose $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = M$$ , where $$L$$ and $$M$$ are real numbers. What conditions on $$L$$ , $$M$$ , and $$f(a)$$ will guarantee that $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ ?

5. Determine whether each function $$f$$ is continuous or discontinuous. Explain your answer. $$f(t)$$ gives the altitude of an airplane at time $$t$$ . $$f(t)$$ measures the total amount of rainfall at time $$t$$ at the Municipal Airport. $$f(s)$$ measures the fare as a function of the distance $$s$$ for taking a cab from Kennedy Airport to downtown Manhattan. $$f(t)$$ gives the interest rate charged by a financial institution at time $$t$$ .
6. Explain the Intermediate Value Theorem in your own words.

solution.paragraph: Michael makes progress toward solving the problem until $$x = x_{1}$$ . Between $$x = x_{1}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ , he makes no further progress. But at $$x = x_{2}$$ he suddenly achieves a breakthrough, and at $$x = x_{3}$$ he proceeds to complete the problem.

problem.paragraph: Weiss’s Law According to Weiss’s law of excitation of tissue, the strength $$S$$ of an electric current is related to the time $$t$$ the current takes to excite tissue by the formula

list.item: Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}S(t)$$ and interpret your result.

solution.paragraph: $$\infty$$ ; as the time taken to excite the tissue is made shorter and shorter, the strength of the electric current gets stronger and stronger.
$$b$$ ; as the time taken to excite the tissue is made longer and longer, the strength of the electric current gets weaker and weaker and approaches $$b$$ .

list.item: Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to conclude that the ball must cross Joan’s line of sight at least once.

section.heading: Using Technology Finding the Points of Discontinuity of a Function
section.paragraph: You can very often recognize the points of discontinuity of a function $$f$$ by examining its graph. For example, Figure T1a shows the graph of $$f(x) = x \slash (x^{2} - 1)$$ obtained using a graphing utility. It is evident that $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 1$$ . This observation is also borne out by the fact that both these points are not in the domain of $$f$$ .

section.heading: 2.6. The Derivative
An Intuitive Example
section.paragraph: We mentioned in Section 2.4 that the problem of finding the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another is mathematically equivalent to the problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve. Before going on to establish this relationship, let’s show its plausibility by looking at it from an intuitive point of view.
Consider the motion of the maglev discussed in Section 2.4. Recall that the position of the maglev at any time $$t$$ is given by
where $$s$$ is measured in feet and $$t$$ in seconds. The graph of the function $$f$$ is sketched in Figure 48.

image.alt: Details A curve s = f(t) is graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t ranges from around 0 to about 4 seconds. The vertical axis s ranges from below 0 to over 60 feet. The curve begins at the origin, rises upward to the right, increasingly bulging away from the y axis, as it rises upward to the right into the first quadrant till around (4.2, 80).

figure.caption: Graph showing the position $$s$$ of a maglev at time $$t$$

section.paragraph: Observe that the graph of $$f$$ rises slowly at first but more rapidly as $$t$$ increases, reflecting the fact that the speed of the maglev is increasing with time. This observation suggests a relationship between the speed of the maglev at any time $$t$$ and the steepness of the curve at the point corresponding to this value of $$t$$ . Thus, it would appear that we can solve the problem of finding the speed of the maglev at any time if we can find a way to measure the steepness of the curve at any point on the curve.

To discover a yardstick that will measure the steepness of a curve, consider the graph of a function $$f$$ such as the one shown in Figure 49a. Think of the curve as representing a stretch of roller coaster track (Figure 49b). When the car is at the point $$P$$ on the curve, a passenger sitting erect in the car and looking straight ahead will have a line of sight that is parallel to the line $$T$$ , the tangent to the curve at $$P$$ .

image.alt: Details Two images a and b Image a: A curve y = f(x) and its tangent T are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the bottom right of the first quadrant, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, reaches a high point and then descends to the right, reaches a low point and then rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. A line is drawn entirely above the curve with a positive slope. It begins near the y axis, rises upward to the right and touches the curve at a point labeled P(x, f(x)) when it first rises upward to the right. Image b: The exact same curve and the tangent are drawn in Image b with only the curve and the tangent labeled y = f(x) and T respectively. Below the curve, equidistant vertical, horizontal and slanted lines running upward to the right and downward to the left are drawn below the curve forming a grid. Above the tangent, the silhouettes of the busts of three people are drawn. A line segment is drawn parallel to the tangent labeled line of sight.

section.paragraph: As Figure 49a suggests, the steepness of the curve—that is, the rate at which $$y$$ is increasing or decreasing with respect to $$x$$ —is given by the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ . But for now we will show how this relationship can be used to estimate the rate of change of a function from its graph.

note.paragraph: Use the graph of $$y = N(t)$$ to estimate the rate at which the number of Social Security beneficiaries was growing at the beginning of the year 2000 $$(t = 10)$$ . How fast will the number be growing at the beginning of 2025 $$(t = 35)$$ ? [Assume that the rate of change of the function $$N$$ at any value of $$t$$ is given by the slope of the tangent line at the point $$P\left( t,N(t) \right)$$ .]
Source: Social Security Administration.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: From the figure, we see that the slope of the tangent line $$T_{1}$$ to the graph of $$y = N(t)$$ at $$P_{1}(10,44.7)$$ is approximately $$0.5$$ . This tells us that the quantity $$y$$ is increasing at the rate of $$\frac{1}{2}$$ unit per unit increase in $$t$$ , when $$t = 10$$ . In other words, at the beginning of the year 2000, the number of Social Security beneficiaries was increasing at the rate of approximately $$0.5$$ millon, or $$500,000$$ , per year.

The slope of the tangent line $$T_{2}$$ at $$P_{2}(35,71.9)$$ is approximately $$1.15$$ . This tells us that at the beginning of 2025 the number of Social Security beneficiaries will be growing at the rate of approximately $$1.15$$ million, or $$1,150,000$$ , per year.

section.heading: Slope of a Tangent Line
section.paragraph: In Example 1, we answered the questions raised by drawing the graph of the function $$N$$ and estimating the position of the tangent lines. Ideally, however, we would like to solve a problem analytically whenever possible. To do this, we need a precise definition of the slope of a tangent line to a curve.

To define the tangent line to a curve $$C$$ at a point $$P$$ on the curve, fix $$P$$ and let $$Q$$ be any point on $$C$$ distinct from $$P$$ (Figure 51). The straight line passing through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ is called a secant line .

image.alt: Details A curve C is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging down, reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)),continues to rise upward to the right into the first quadrant, bulging towards the x axis. A point labeled Q is located near the top right of the curve. Three unlabelled points are marked on the curve between P and Q. Four lines rising upward to the right are drawn passing through P and each of the other 4 points. All four lines are together labeled Secant lines. One line is drawn entirely below the curve. It starts from the bottom left, touches the curve at P(x, f(x)) and then gradually rises upward to the right.

figure.caption: As $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ along the curve $$C$$ , the secant lines approach the tangent line $$T$$ .

section.paragraph: Now, as the point $$Q$$ is allowed to move toward $$P$$ along the curve, the secant line through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ rotates about the fixed point $$P$$ and approaches a fixed line through $$P$$ . This fixed line, which is the limiting position of the secant lines through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ as $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ , is the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P$$ .

We can describe the process more precisely as follows. Suppose the curve $$C$$ is the graph of a function $$f$$ defined by $$y = f(x)$$ . Then the point $$P$$ is described by $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and the point $$Q$$ by $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ , where $$h$$ is some appropriate nonzero number (Figure 52a). Observe that we can make $$Q$$ approach $$P$$ along the curve $$C$$ by letting $$h$$ approach zero (Figure 52b).

image.alt: Details The image has two graphs. On the left, a curve C defined by y = f(x) and a line graphed are in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging downward and reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)), rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis, passes through another point labeled Q((x + h), f(x + h)) and continues into the first quadrant. From the point P(x, f(x)), a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis, meeting it at the mark labeled x. From the point Q ((x + h), f(x + h)), a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis, meeting it at the mark labeled x + h. A line begins near the x axis, rises upward to the right and cuts the curve at two points: P(x, f(x)), Q ((x + h), f(x + h)). The second curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging downward and reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)), rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis, and continues into the first quadrant. The points P, situated near the bottom left of the curve, and Q, located near the top right of the curve, are labeled. Three unlabelled points are marked on the curve between P and Q. The horizontal distance between P and each of the other points is labeled h.

section.paragraph: Next, using the formula for the slope of a line, we can write the slope of the secant line passing through $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ as
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{(x + h) - x} = \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

As we observed earlier, $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ , and therefore the secant line through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ approaches the tangent line $$T$$ as $$h$$ approaches zero. Consequently, we might expect that the slope of the secant line would approach the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ as $$h$$ approaches zero. This leads to the following definition.

note.title: Slope of a Tangent Line
note.heading: Slope of a Tangent Line
note.paragraph: The slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is given by
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
if it exists.

section.heading: Rates of Change
section.paragraph: We now show that the problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to the graph of a function $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is mathematically equivalent to the problem of finding the rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . To see this, suppose we are given a function $$f$$ that describes the relationship between the two quantities $$x$$ and $$y$$ —that is, $$y = f(x)$$ . The number $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ measures the change in $$y$$ that corresponds to a change $$h$$ in $$x$$ (Figure 53).

image.alt: Details A curve y = f(x) is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis, descends to the right bulging down, reaches a low point and continues to rise upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. From a mark labeled f(x) on the y axis, a line parallel to the x axis runs to the right cutting the curve at two points, the one on the right is labeled P(x, f(x)). From this point a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a point labeled x. From a mark labeled f(x + h) on the y axis, above the mark f(x), another horizontal line runs to the right, parallel to the x axis, and meets the curve at a point marked Q(x + h, f(x + h)). From this point a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a mark labeled x + h. The distance between the two perpendiculars to the x axis reaching the x axis at x and x + h, is labeled h. The distance between the two lines parallel to the x axis at f(x) and f(x + h) is labeled f(x + h) – f(x).

figure.caption: $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ is the change in $$y$$ that corresponds to a change $$h$$ in $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Then, the difference quotient
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

measures the average rate of change of $$\mathbf{y}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ over the interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ . For example, if $$y$$ measures the position of a car at time $$x$$ , then quotient (7) gives the average velocity of the car over the time interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ .

Observe that the difference quotient (7) is the same as (5). We conclude that the difference quotient (7) also measures the slope of the secant line that passes through the two points $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ lying on the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ . Next, by taking the limit of the difference quotient (7) as $$h$$ goes to zero—that is, by evaluating
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

we obtain the rate of change of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ . For example, if $$y$$ measures the position of a car at time $$x$$ , then the limit (8) gives the velocity of the car at time $$x$$ . For emphasis, the rate of change of a function $$f$$ at $$x$$ is often called the instantaneous rate of change of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ . This distinguishes it from the average rate of change of $$f$$ , which is computed over an interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ rather than at a number $$x$$ .

Observe that the limit (8) is the same as (6). Therefore, the limit of the difference quotient also measures the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ . The following summarizes this discussion.

note.source_type: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.title: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.heading: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.paragraph: The average rate of change of $$f$$ over the interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ or slope of the secant line to the graph of $$f$$ through the points $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ is
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
The instantaneous rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ or slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow\infty}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

note.title: Explore and Discuss
note.heading: Explore and Discuss
note.paragraph: Explain the difference between the average rate of change of a function and the instantaneous rate of change of a function.

section.heading: The Derivative
section.paragraph: The limit $$(6)$$ or $$(10)$$ , which measures both the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and the (instantaneous) rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ , is given a special name: the derivative of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ .

note.title: Derivative of a Function
note.heading: Derivative of a Function
note.paragraph: The derivative of a function $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ is the function $$f^{\prime}$$ (read “ $$f$$ prime”),
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
The domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ is the set of all $$x$$ for which the limit exists.

section.paragraph: Thus, the derivative of a function $$f$$ is a function $$f^{\prime}$$ that gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at any point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and also the rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ (Figure 54).

image.alt: Details A curve y = f(x) and a line T are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins in the second quadrant at a distance above the negative x axis, rises upward to the right, cuts the y axis, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, reaches a peak and then descends to the right, reaches a low point and then rises upward, passing through a labeled point P(x, f(x)) now bulging down towards the x axis. The line begins near the x axis, rises upward to the right with a positive slope and touches the curve near its second inflection point as it rises to the right. The point where the tangent touches the curve is labeled P(x, f(x)). A vertical line segment from the mark x rises upward from the x axis, parallel to the y axis and meets the curve and the line at P(x, f(x)). Another line segment starts from P, runs horizontally to the right parallel to the x axis accompanied by the text 1. From the end of this line segment, another line segment runs vertically upward accompanied by the text f prime (x).

figure.caption: The slope of the tangent line at $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ ; $$f$$ changes at the rate of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ units per unit change in $$x$$ at $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Other notations for the derivative of $$f$$ include the following:
$$\begin{array}{ll} {D_{x}f(x)} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}{sub}x{of}f{of}x^{"}}} \\ \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}ydx^{"}}} \\ y^{\prime} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}{prime}^{"}}} \end{array}$$
The last two are used when the rule for $$f$$ is written in the form $$y = f(x)$$ .
The calculation of the derivative of $$f$$ is facilitated by using the following four-step process.

note.source_type: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )
note.title: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )
note.heading: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )

list.item: Compute $$f(x + h)$$ .
Form the difference $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ .
Form the quotient $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$ .
Compute the limit $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 3x + 5$$ at any point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The slope of the tangent line at any point on the graph of $$f$$ is given by the derivative of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . To find the derivative, we use the four-step process:
example.heading: Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
example.paragraph: We expect this result, since the tangent line to any point on a straight line must coincide with the line itself and therefore must have the same slope as the line. In this case, the graph of $$f$$ is a straight line with slope 3.

list.item: Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
Compute $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ and interpret your result.

To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f(x + h) = (x + h)^{2} = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2}$$ Step 2 $$f(x + h) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - x^{2} = 2xh + h^{2} = h(2x + h)$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \frac{h(2x + h)}{h} = 2x + h$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}(2x + h) = 2x$$

$$f^{\prime}(2) = 2(2) = 4$$ . This result tells us that the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$(2,4)$$ is $$4$$ . It also tells us that the function $$f$$ is changing at the rate of $$4$$ units per unit change in $$x$$ at $$x = 2$$ . The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line at $$(2,4)$$ are shown in Figure 55.

image.alt: Details A curve y = x^2, an upward opening parabola with its vertex at the origin, and its tangent are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from about negative 3 to around 3 units. The y axis ranges from below negative 1 to over 7 units. The curve descends into the second quadrant at around (negative 2.8, 7.4), continues its descent to the right, bulging away from the y axis, reaches a low point at the origin, and then rises upward to the right in the first quadrant, bulging away from the y axis, mirroring its earlier path, symmetric about the y axis. At a marked point (2, 4) a tangent is drawn to the curve. The line enters the third quadrant around (0.5, negative 1.5), rises upward to the right, cuts the x axis at (1, 0), continues to rise upward to the right, touches the curve at (2, 4) and then continues to rise upward to the right.

figure.caption: The tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ at $$(2,4)$$

list.item: Consider the function $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ of Example 3. Suppose we want to compute $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ , using Equation (11). Thus, $$f^{\prime}(2) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {2 + h} \right) - f(2)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {2 + h} \right)^{2} - 2^{2}}{h}$$ Use a graphing utility to plot the graph of $$g(x) = \frac{\left( {2 + x} \right)^{2} - 4}{x}$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 3,3\rbrack \times \lbrack - 2,6\rbrack$$ .
Use zoom and trace to find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ .
Explain why the limit found in part 2 is $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ .
Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
Find the point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal.
Sketch the graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line to the curve at the point found in part (b).
What is the rate of change of $$f$$ at this point?

To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f\left( {x + h} \right) = \left( {x + h} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {x + h} \right) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h$$ Step 2 $$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h - {({x^{2} - 4x})}} \\ {\phantom{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)} = 2\mathit{xh} + h^{2} - 4h = h\left( {2x + h - 4} \right)} \end{array}$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \frac{h{({2x + h - 4})}}{h} = 2x + h - 4$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({2x + h - 4})} = 2x - 4$$

At a point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal and hence has slope zero, the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of $$f$$ is zero. Accordingly, to find such point(s), we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , which gives $$2x - 4 = 0$$ or $$x = 2$$ . The corresponding value of $$y$$ is given by $$y = f(2) = - 4$$ , and the required point is $$(2, - 4)$$ .

The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line are shown in Figure 56. Figure 56 Details A curve y = x^2 minus 4 x, an open upward parabola with its vertex at (2, negative 4) and its tangent y = negative 4 are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from around negative 1 to about 5 units. The y axis ranges from below negative 5 to over 3 units. The curve enters the second quadrant at around (negative 0.8, 3.5), descends downward to the right,, passes through the origin, descends downward into the fourth quadrant, inflects at (2, negative 4), and rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. The curve then cuts the x axis at (4, 0) and continues rising upward to the right, into the first quadrant. A horizontal line y = negative 4 runs to the right, parallel to the x axis enters the third quadrant, cuts the y axis at the negative 4 mark, touches the curve at (2, negative 4) as it continues into the fourth quadrant. The tangent line to the graph of $$y = x^{2} - 4x$$ at $$\left( {2, - 4} \right)$$ is $$y = - 4$$ .
The rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x = 2$$ is zero.

list.item: Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
Find the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the graph of $$f$$ at the point where $$x = 1$$ .
Find an equation of the tangent line $$T$$ in part (b).

To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f\left( {x + h} \right) = \frac{1}{x + h}$$ Step 2 $$f{({x + h})} - f{(x)} = \frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x} = \frac{x - {({x + h})}}{x{({x + h})}} = - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}}$$ Algebra See Example 3. Step 3 $$\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}} \cdot \frac{1}{h} = - \frac{1}{x{({x + h})}}$$ Algebra See Example 3. Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0} - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}} = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$
The slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the graph of $$f$$ where $$x = 1$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(1) = - 1$$ .

When $$x = 1$$ , $$y = f(1) = 1$$ and $$T$$ is tangent to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$(1,1)$$ . From part (b), we know that the slope of $$T$$ is $$- 1$$ . Thus, an equation of $$T$$ is $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - 1} & = & {- 1\left( {x - 1} \right)} \\ y & = & {- x + 2} \end{array}$$ (Figure 57). Figure 57 Details A curve y = 1/x and a line y = negative x + 2 are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve has two parts. One part of the curve is entirely in the third quadrant and enters close to the negative x axis almost parallel to it, veering off the axis at around (negative 4, 0.25), descends to the right bulging towards the origin, continues to descend downward steeply, becoming almost parallel to the negative y axis as it descends downward. The second part of the curve lies entirely in the first quadrant, enters close the to the y axis, almost parallel to it, increasingly veering off the y axis from about (0.2, 4), descends to the right, passing through a low point (1, 1) bulging towards the origin, descends to the right, running almost parallel to the x axis as it proceeds further to the right. The tangent to the curve y = negative x + 2, descends into the second quadrant at around (2.8, 5), slopes downward to the right, cuts the y axis at (0, 3), touches the curve at (1, 1), cuts the x axis at (2, 0) and then proceeds to slope downward into the fourth quadrant. The tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ at $$(1,1)$$

note.source_type: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.title: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.paragraph: Suppose the distance (in feet) covered by a car moving along a straight road $$t$$ seconds after starting from rest is given by the function $$f(t) = 2t^{2}\left( {0 \leq t \leq 30} \right)$$ .

list.item: Calculate the average velocity of the car over the time intervals $$\lbrack 22,23\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack 22,22.1\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack 22,22.01\rbrack$$ .
Calculate the (instantaneous) velocity of the car when $$t = 22$$ .
Compare the results obtained in part (a) with that obtained in part (b).

note.heading: Solution

list.item: We first compute the average velocity (average rate of change of $$f$$ ) over the interval $$\lbrack t,t + h\rbrack$$ using Formula (9). We find $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h} = \frac{2\left( {t + h} \right)^{2} - 2t^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = \frac{2t^{2} + 4th + 2h^{2} - 2t^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = 4t + 2h} \end{array}$$ Next, using $$t = 22$$ and $$h = 1$$ , we find that the average velocity of the car over the time interval $$\lbrack 22,23\rbrack$$ is $$4(22) + 2(1) = 90$$ or $$90{ft}/\sec$$ . Similarly, using $$t = 22$$ , $$h = 0.1$$ , and $$h = 0.01$$ , we find that its average velocities over the time intervals $$\lbrack 22,22.1\rbrack$$ and $$\lbrack 22,22.01\rbrack$$ are $$88.2$$ and $$88.02{ft}/\sec$$ , respectively.

Using the limit $$(10)$$ , we see that the instantaneous velocity of the car at any time $$t$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {4t + 2h} \right) { \text{Use the results from part} (a).}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = 4t} \end{array}$$ In particular, the velocity of the car $$22$$ seconds from rest $$(t = 22)$$ is given by $$\upsilon = 4(22)$$ or $$88{ft}/\sec$$ .

The computations in part (a) show that, as the time intervals over which the average velocity of the car are computed become smaller and smaller, the average velocities over these intervals do approach $$88{ft}/\sec$$ , the instantaneous velocity of the car at $$t = 22$$ .

note.paragraph: The management of Titan Tire Company has determined that the weekly demand function of their Super Titan tires is given by
where $$p$$ , the price per tire, is measured in dollars and $$x$$ is measured in units of a thousand (Figure 58).

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on a coordinate plane where the horizontal axis x ranges from 0 to over 15 thousand units and the vertical axis p ranges from 0 to over 200 dollars. The curve begins from the y axis at approximately (0, 150), descends downward to the right, bulging away from the x axis and converging towards the axis till it meets the x axis at (11, 0).

figure.caption: The graph of the demand function $$p = 144 - x^{2}$$

list.item: Find the average rate of change in the unit price of a tire if the quantity demanded is between $$5000$$ and $$6000$$ tires, between $$5000$$ and $$5100$$ tires, and between $$5000$$ and $$5010$$ tires.
What is the instantaneous rate of change of the unit price when the quantity demanded is $$5000$$ units?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The average rate of change of the unit price of a tire if the quantity demanded (in thousands) is between $$x$$ and $$x + h$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \frac{\lbrack 144 - {({x + h})}^{2}\rbrack - ({144 - x^{2}})}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h}} = \frac{144 - x^{2} - 2xh - h^{2} - 144 + x^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h}} = - 2x - h} \end{array}$$ To find the average rate of change of the unit price of a tire when the quantity demanded is between $$5000$$ and $$6000$$ tires (that is, over the interval $$\lbrack 5,6\rbrack$$ ), we take $$x = 5$$ and $$h = 1$$ , obtaining $$- 2(5) - 1 = - 11$$ or $$- \$ 11$$ per $$1000$$ tires. (Remember, $$x$$ is measured in units of a thousand.) Similarly, taking $$h = 0.1$$ and $$h = 0.01$$ with $$x = 5$$ , we find that the average rates of change of the unit price when the quantities demanded are between $$5000$$ and $$5100$$ and between $$5000$$ and $$5010$$ are $$- \$ 10.10$$ and $$- \$ 10.01$$ per $$1000$$ tires, respectively.

The instantaneous rate of change of the unit price of a tire when the quantity demanded is $$x$$ units is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {- 2x - h} \right) { \text{Use the results from part} (a).}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}} = - 2x} \end{array}$$ In particular, the instantaneous rate of change of the unit price per tire when the quantity demanded is $$5000$$ is given by $$- 2(5)$$ , or $$- \$ 10$$ per $$1000$$ tires.

section.heading: Differentiability and Continuity
section.paragraph: In practical applications, one encounters continuous functions that fail to be differentiable —that is, do not have a derivative—at certain values in the domain of the function $$f$$ . It can be shown that a continuous function $$f$$ fails to be differentiable at $$x = a$$ when the graph of $$f$$ makes an abrupt change of direction at $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ . We call such a point a “corner.” A function also fails to be differentiable at a point where the tangent line is vertical, since the slope of a vertical line is undefined. These cases are illustrated in Figure 59.

image.alt: Details There are two graphs a and b. In image a, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. It begins in the second quadrant close to the negative x axis in the bottom left, rises upward to the right, bulging slightly upward intersecting the y axis at an unmarked point till it reaches a peak at a point marked (a, f(a)). From here, the curve descends downward to the right, bulging slightly downward. From the peak point, a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a labeled point a. In image b, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. From the x axis, at a mark labeled a, a line extends vertically upward, parallel to the y axis, cutting the curve at (a, f(a)). The curve begins near the x axis in the first quadrant a little away from the origin, rises upward to the right, bulging towards the x axis, briefly straightens out as it meets the line x = a, at the point labeled (a, f(a)), after which it rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis.

section.paragraph: The next example illustrates a function that is not differentiable at a point.

note.title: Applied Example 8. Wages
note.heading: Applied Example 8. Wages
note.paragraph: Mary works at the B&O department store, where, on a weekday, she is paid $$\$ 10$$ an hour for the first $$8$$ hours and $$\$ 15$$ an hour for overtime. The function
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} {10x} & { {if}0 \leq x \leq 8} \\ {15x - 40} & { {if}8 < x} \end{cases}$$
gives Mary’s earnings on a weekday in which she worked $$x$$ hours. Sketch the graph of the function $$f$$ , and explain why it is not differentiable at $$x = 8$$ .
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure 60. Observe that the graph of $$f$$ has a corner at $$x = 8$$ and consequently is not differentiable at $$x = 8$$ .

image.alt: Details A line is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to over 12 hours. The y axis ranges from 0 to over 140 dollars. The line begins at the origin, rises upward to the right till the labeled point (8, 80). From here, the line deviates to the left, rising up again linearly but with a steeper slope.

figure.caption: The function $$f$$ is not differentiable at $$(8,80)$$ .

section.paragraph: We close this section by mentioning the connection between the continuity and the differentiability of a function at a given value $$x = a$$ in the domain of $$f$$ . By reexamining the function of Example 8, it becomes clear that $$f$$ is continuous everywhere and, in particular, when $$x = 8$$ . This shows that in general the continuity of a function at $$x = a$$ does not necessarily imply the differentiability of the function at that number. The converse, however, is true: If a function $$f$$ is differentiable at $$x = a$$ , then it is continuous there.

note.title: Differentiability and Continuity
note.heading: Differentiability and Continuity
note.paragraph: If a function is differentiable at $$x = a$$ , then it is continuous at $$x = a$$ .

section.paragraph: For a proof of this result, see Exercise 62.

example.paragraph: Figure 61 depicts a portion of the graph of a function. Explain why the function fails to be differentiable at each of the numbers $$x = a,b,c,d,e,f$$ , and $$g$$ .

image.alt: Details A function is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. Line segments from the x axis rise upward to meet the curve at the labeled points a, b, c, d, e, f, and g. The intervals between the line segments are not equal. The curve begins from the third quadrant, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, cuts the x axis, enters into the second quadrant, cuts the y axis, continues upward to the right till it reaches the line segment from x = a where it ends with an open circle. The next part of the curve begins with a closed circle directly above the open circle on the line x = a, descends downward to the right, bulging downward, towards the x axis, till it meets the line at x = b with an open circle where it inflects and then continues to rise steeply upward to the right running almost parallel to the line at x = c. From the line x = c a little above the inflection point of the previous segment of the curve, a line segment begins with a closed circle, runs horizontally to the right parallel to the x axis to meet the line at x = d. From x = d, a line segment rises up to the right till it meets the vertical line at x = e. From this point, the line slopes downward to the left till it reaches the line at x = f. From this point, a curve rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis at first, reaches a peak and then descends to the right, bulging down, reaches a low point and then steeply rises to meet the line at x = g. From x = g, the curve arches upward and almost levels out at the top right.

figure.caption: The graph of this function is not differentiable at the numbers $$a - g$$ .

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The function fails to be differentiable at $$x = a,b$$ , and $$c$$ because it is discontinuous at each of these numbers. The derivative of the function does not exist at $$x = d,e$$ , and $$f$$ because it has a kink at each point on the graph corresponding to these numbers. Finally, the function is not differentiable at $$x = g$$ because the tangent line is vertical at the corresponding point on the graph.

problem.paragraph: Bank Losses The losses (in millions of dollars) due to bad loans extended chiefly in agriculture, real estate, shipping, and energy by the Franklin Bank are estimated to be
where $$t$$ is the time in years ( $$t = 0$$ corresponds to the beginning of 2007). How fast were the losses mounting at the beginning of 2010? At the beginning of 2012? At the beginning of 2014?

solution.paragraph: The rate of change of the losses at any time $$t$$ is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(t) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(t + h) - f(t)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)}{= \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\lbrack - {(t + h)}^{2} + 10(t + h) + 30\rbrack - ( - t^{2} + 10t + 30)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)}{= \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- t^{2} - 2\mathit{th} - h^{2} + 10t + 10h + 30 + t^{2} - 10t - 30}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)}{= \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h( - 2t - h + 10)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)}{= \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}( - 2t - h + 10)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)}{= - 2t + 10}} \end{array}$$
Therefore, the rate of change of the losses suffered by the bank at the beginning of 2010 $$(t = 3)$$ was
In other words, the losses were increasing at the rate of $${\$ 4}{{million} \slash {year}}$$ . At the beginning of 2012 $$(t = 5)$$ ,
and we see that the growth in losses due to bad loans was zero at this point. At the beginning of 2014 $$(t = 7)$$ ,
and we conclude that the losses were decreasing at the rate of $$\$ 4{million} \slash {year}$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Use the numerical derivative operation of a graphing calculator to find the derivative of $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ when $$x = 2$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Access the numerical derivative operation, nDeriv, by pressing $$\boxed{\mathbf{MATH}}\boxed{8}$$ . The display nDeriv( appears on the screen. Next, we enter the function whose derivative we want to find, the variable $$x$$ , followed by the value of $$x$$ at which the derivative is to be evaluated, and then press $$\boxed{\mathbf{ENTER}}$$ . The approximate derivative of $$f$$ at $$x = 2$$ is shown on the screen (Figure T1).

section.heading: Chapter 2. Concept Review Questions
section.paragraph: Fill in the blanks.

list.item: 1. If $$f$$ is a function from the set $$A$$ to the set $$B$$ , then $$A$$ is called the domain of $$f$$ , and the set of all values of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ takes on all possible values in $$A$$ is called the range of $$f$$ . The range of $$f$$ is contained in the set $$B$$ .

2. The graph of a function is the set of all points $$(x,y)$$ in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane such that $$x$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ and $$y =$$ $$f(x)$$ . The Vertical Line Test states that a curve in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the graph of a function $$y = f(x)$$ if and only if each vertical line intersects it in at most one point.

3. If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are functions with domains $$A$$ and $$B$$ , respectively, then (a) $$\left( {f \pm g} \right)(x) =$$ $$f(x) \pm g(x)$$ , (b) $$\left( \mathit{fg} \right)(x) =$$ $$f(x)g(x)$$ , and (c) $$\left( {f \slash g} \right)(x) =$$ $$\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$ . The domain of $$f + g$$ is $$A \cap B$$ . The domain of $$f \slash g$$ is $$A \cap B$$ with the additional condition that $$g(x)$$ is never $$0$$ .

4. The composition of $$g$$ and $$f$$ is the function with rule $$(g \circ f)(x) =$$ $$g\lbrack f(x)\rbrack$$ . Its domain is the set of all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that $$f(x)$$ lies in the domain of $$g$$ .

5. A polynomial function of degree $$n$$ is a function of the form $$P(x) = a_{n}x^{n} + a_{n - 1}x^{n - 1} + \cdots + a_{1}x + a_{0}(a_{n} \neq 0,n,a{positive}{integer})$$ . A polynomial function of degree $$1$$ is called a/an linear function; one of degree $$2$$ is called a/an quadratic function; one of degree $$3$$ is called a/an cubic function. A rational function is a/an quotient of two polynomials. A power function has the form $$f(x) =$$ $$x^{r}$$ ( $$r$$ a real number).
6. The statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ means that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$L$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to $$a$$ .

7. If $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = M$$ , then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{r} =$$ $$L^{r}$$ , where $$r$$ is a positive constant. $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) \pm g(x)} \right\rbrack =$$ $$L \pm M$$ . $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack =$$ LM . $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} =$$ $$\frac{L}{M}$$ provided that $$M \neq 0$$ .

8. The statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$ means that $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by taking $$x$$ large enough. The statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = M$$ means that $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$M$$ by taking $$x$$ to be negative and sufficiently large in absolute value.

9. The statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = L$$ is similar to the statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ , but here $$x$$ is required to lie to the right of $$a$$ . The statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$ is similar to the statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ , but here $$x$$ is required to lie to the left of $$a$$ . $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ if and only if both $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) =$$ $$L$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) =$$ $$L$$ .

10. If $$f(a)$$ is defined, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)$$ exists and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = f(a)$$ , then $$f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ . If $$f$$ is not continuous at $$a$$ , then it is discontinuous at $$a$$ . $$f$$ is continuous on an interval $$I$$ if $$f$$ is continuous at every number in the interval.

11. If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous at $$a$$ , then $$f \pm g$$ and $$\mathit{fg}$$ are continuous at $$a$$ . Also, $$f \slash g$$ is continuous at $$a$$ , provided $$g(a)$$ $$\neq 0$$ . A polynomial function is continuous everywhere. A rational function $$R = P \slash Q$$ is continuous everywhere except at values of $$x$$ for which $$Q(x)$$ $$= 0$$ .

12. Suppose $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$f(a) < M < f(b)$$ . Then the intermediate value theorem guarantees the existence of at least one number $$c$$ in $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ such that $$f(c) = M$$ . If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$f(a)f(b) < 0$$ , then there must be at least one solution of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ in the interval $$(a,b)$$ .

13. The tangent line at $$P\left( a,f(a) \right)$$ to the graph of $$f$$ is the line passing through $$P$$ and having slope $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ . If the slope of the tangent line at $$P\left( a,f(a) \right)$$ is $$m$$ , then an equation of the tangent line at $$P$$ is $$y = f(a) + m(x - a)$$ .

14. The slope of the secant line passing through $$P\left( a,f(a) \right)$$ and $$Q\left( a + h,f(a + h) \right)$$ and the average rate of change of $$f$$ over the interval $$\lbrack a,a + h\rbrack$$ are both given by $$\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$ . The slope of the tangent line at $$P\left( a,f(a) \right)$$ and the instantaneous rate of change of $$f$$ at $$a$$ are both given by $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$ .

Manufacturing Costs Suppose that the total cost of manufacturing $$x$$ units of a certain product is $$C(x)$$ dollars.

list.item: What does $$C^{\prime}(x)$$ measure? Give units.
What can you say about the sign of $$C^{\prime}$$ ?
Given that $$C^{\prime}(1000) = 20$$ , estimate the additional cost to be incurred by the company in producing the 1001st unit of the product.

solution.paragraph: $$C^{\prime}(x)$$ gives the instantaneous rate of change of the total manufacturing cost $$C$$ in dollars with respect to the quantity produced when $$x$$ units of the product are produced.

exercises.paragraph: The problem-solving skills that you learn in each chapter are building blocks for the rest of the course. Therefore, it is a good idea to make sure that you have mastered these skills before moving on to the next chapter. The Before Moving On exercises that follow are designed for that purpose. After completing these exercises, you can identify the skills that you should review before starting the next chapter.
